undetected_forms.text: an action whose code puts a file that holds secrets of the job in a place where others read the file: the debug artifact of github/codeql-action, which holds the environment of the job (GHSA-vqf5-2xx6-9wfm), or the cache of GitHub Actions, where gradle/gradle-build-action saves the configuration cache of Gradle, which a run of a pull request from a fork restores (GHSA-h3qr-39j9-4r5v); known-vulnerable-actions reports a step that uses a version in the range of such an advisory

examples.name: action-code.yml
examples.text:
# situation: two jobs use actions whose own code puts a file that holds
#   secrets of the job in a place where others read the file, in the forms of
#   two advisories, which name no workflow. The job codeql is the form of
#   GHSA-vqf5-2xx6-9wfm: github/codeql-action v3.28.2 with debug artifacts
#   turned on analyzes Java and Kotlin, and the CodeQL CLI writes the
#   environment variables of the job, the GITHUB_TOKEN among them, into an
#   intermediate file, which the action uploads in the debug artifact when the
#   analysis fails ("debug artifacts uploaded by the CodeQL Action after a
#   failed code scanning workflow run may contain the environment variables from
#   the workflow run, including any secrets that were exposed as environment
#   variables"). The job gradle is the form of GHSA-h3qr-39j9-4r5v:
#   gradle/gradle-build-action v2.4.1 runs a build with the configuration cache
#   of Gradle, which records the environment variables, the secret of the job
#   among them, and the action saves the configuration cache to the cache of
#   GitHub Actions ("This data stored in the GitHub Actions cache can be read by
#   a GitHub Actions workflow running in an untrusted context, such as that
#   running for a Pull Request submitted by a developer via a repository fork").
# reason: one who can read the repository downloads the debug artifact while
#   the job runs, and a run of a pull request from a fork restores the cache of
#   the default branch; both read the secrets of the job. The rule reports
#   neither form, but known-vulnerable-actions reports each step that uses a
#   version in the range of the advisory (codeql-action from 3.26.11 to 3.28.2,
#   gradle-build-action before 2.4.2), so the user learns that the version is
#   vulnerable.
# cause: the rule checks only the steps that use actions/upload-artifact, and
#   does not read what the code of an action writes and where the code puts the
#   file.
# attack: one who can read the repository downloads the debug artifact of a
#   failed analysis (the job codeql); the author of a pull request from a fork
#   changes the build of the pull request to print the files of the
#   configuration cache that the run restores (the job gradle).
# attack-run-behavior: the debug artifact holds the GITHUB_TOKEN of the job
#   codeql, which is valid until the job ends; the restored configuration cache
#   holds the value of the secret GRADLE_PUBLISH_KEY.
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vqf5-2xx6-9wfm
# advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3qr-39j9-4r5v
on: push
permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write
jobs:
  codeql:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@d68b2d4edb4189fd2a5366ac14e72027bd4b37dd # v3.28.2
        with:
          languages: java-kotlin
          debug: true
      - run: ./gradlew build
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@d68b2d4edb4189fd2a5366ac14e72027bd4b37dd # v3.28.2
  gradle:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: gradle/gradle-build-action@5056fa9d50478a14af3c9925c12ca02318659d3e # v2.4.1
        with:
          arguments: build --configuration-cache
        env:
          GRADLE_PUBLISH_KEY: ${{ secrets.GRADLE_PUBLISH_KEY }}

The job codeql is the form of GHSA-vqf5-2xx6-9wfm: github/codeql-action v3.28.2 with debug artifacts turned on analyzes Java and Kotlin, and the CodeQL CLI writes the environment variables of the job, the GITHUB_TOKEN among them, into an intermediate file, which the action uploads in the debug artifact when the analysis fails ("debug artifacts uploaded by the CodeQL Action after a failed code scanning workflow run may contain the environment variables from the workflow run, including any secrets that were exposed as environment variables"). The job gradle is the form of GHSA-h3qr-39j9-4r5v: gradle/gradle-build-action v2.4.1 runs a build with the configuration cache of Gradle, which records the environment variables, the secret of the job among them, and the action saves the configuration cache to the cache of GitHub Actions ("This data stored in the GitHub Actions cache can be read by a GitHub Actions workflow running in an untrusted context, such as that running for a Pull Request submitted by a developer via a repository fork").

The rule reports neither form, but known-vulnerable-actions reports each step that uses a version in the range of the advisory (codeql-action from 3.26.11 to 3.28.2, gradle-build-action before 2.4.2), so the user learns that the version is vulnerable.
notes.cause: the rule checks only the steps that use actions/upload-artifact, and does not read what the code of an action writes and where the code puts the file.
notes.attack: one who can read the repository downloads the debug artifact of a failed analysis (the job codeql); the author of a pull request from a fork changes the build of the pull request to print the files of the configuration cache that the run restores (the job gradle).

# situation: on push, the job whose id is disabled has if: false, and the job
#   whose id is on-failure needs the job build and has if: needs.build.result
#   == 'failure'; each of the two jobs calls deploy.yml of
#   octo-org/shared-workflows at @v1 with secrets: inherit.
# reason: GitHub skips the job disabled because the if of the job disabled is
#   false. The if of the job on-failure calls no status function, so GitHub
#   evaluates the if of the job on-failure only when the job build succeeded;
#   needs.build.result is then success, and the if is false. When the job
#   build fails or is skipped, GitHub skips the job on-failure without
#   evaluating the if. So neither job runs
#   (https://github.com/github/docs/blob/404a5f4de6cd5311e3ce2d5c076571291e0107d6/data/reusables/actions/jobs/section-using-conditions-to-control-job-execution.md).
# attack: a maintainer of octo-org/shared-workflows, or whoever takes over an
#   account of a maintainer, moves the tag v1 to a commit whose deploy.yml
#   sends toJSON(secrets) out.
# attack-run-behavior: GitHub skips the job disabled and the job on-failure,
#   so GitHub does not run deploy.yml for the job disabled or for the job
#   on-failure, and passes deploy.yml no secret.
on: push
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo built
  disabled:
    if: false
    uses: octo-org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v1
    secrets: inherit
  on-failure:
    needs: build
    if: needs.build.result == 'failure'
    uses: octo-org/shared-workflows/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v1
    secrets: inherit

notes.attack: a flaw in deploy.yml runs the code of the attacker in a job of deploy.yml.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the account of the attacker is not an allowed actor, so the run on pull_request_target fails with an error, and no job of the run starts (the assumption of the reason), so deploy.yml never gets a secret.

false_positive_forms.text: a workflow whose run GitHub does not start, or a job that GitHub fails in the step "Set up job", because of the setting of allowed actions of GitHub (the fact repo.allowed-actions, which the quality rule allowed-actions reads): GitHub does not start a run of a workflow that has a uses, or that calls a reusable workflow that has a uses, that the setting does not allow, and fails a job before any step of the job runs when a step of a composite action that the job runs has a uses that the setting does not allow, or when the setting requires a full commit SHA and a step names an action by a tag or a branch. The harm that the finding reports happens only when GitHub runs the workflow or the job, and the rule does not read repo.allowed-actions

rules.problem: a repository has a self-hosted runner, which the code of a pull request from a fork reaches, of anyone in a public repository, of whoever may read it in a private or internal one that runs the workflows of such pull requests, and whose state persists for the jobs after it
rules.expected: the jobs on GitHub-hosted runners, or on self-hosted runners that no pull request from a fork reaches; or a private or internal repository that does not run the workflows of pull requests from its forks; or a runs-on with a label whose runners, the owner declares (repo.runner-label-trusted), no pull request from a fork reaches. The rule reads the labels of runs-on only, with the labels a whole ${{ }} gives for each combination of the values of the matrix it reads: the rule does not distinguish an ephemeral runner from another runner, and does not read the settings of a runner group. An ephemeral runner removes the files and the processes that a job leaves on the machine of the runner before the next job, and the code of a pull request still reaches the network of the runner while the job runs

actors.via: opens a pull request whose workflow, which the pull request writes, runs their code on the self-hosted runner

preconditions.text: the repository is private or internal, lets those who may read it fork it (repo.allow-forking) and runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks (repo.fork-pr-run-workflows), a setting of private and internal repositories: those who may read it and fork it, generally those with read access, open such a pull request and compromise the runner; every member of the enterprise reads an internal repository, and the policies of the repository, the organization and the enterprise decide who forks it

the repository is public, so anyone forks it and opens a pull request (repo.public true); by default, the run of a first-time contributor's pull request waits for approval, a contributor's does not; a credential whose only write access is to the permission Actions can approve the run (the endpoint POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/approve), and the credential premise keeps the holder of such a credential as a possible attacker
a pull request from a fork proposes changes to the repository's workflows, and its pull_request run uses them: its author writes the runs-on
a self-hosted runner does not run each job in a clean virtual machine: what a job leaves stays for the jobs after it

incidents.summary: researchers became contributors by a typo fix, then a pull request whose workflow they wrote ran on the self-hosted runners of pytorch/pytorch, where they took secrets and tokens; the repository had jobs on runs-on [self-hosted, linux.2xlarge], and the runner they used had labels of its own

finding_kinds.detected: the job runs on a self-hosted runner ({label}) of a private or internal repository that runs the workflows of pull requests from its forks
finding_kinds.consequence: one who may read the repository and fork it, which every member of the enterprise reads for an internal one, can open a pull request that runs their code on the runner, whose state persists for the jobs after it: their secrets, their tokens and the runner's network
finding_kinds.remedy: turn off Run workflows from fork pull requests, which the rule reads as the fact repo.fork-pr-run-workflows (with the fact false, the rule reports nothing), or run the jobs on GitHub-hosted runners: with a label of a GitHub-hosted runner in runs-on, the rule reports nothing. On self-hosted runners that no pull request from a fork reaches, declare a label of runs-on that only those runners have trusted with the fact repo.runner-label-trusted (true for the label, in a file of facts, --fact, or fact in --config): the rule then reports nothing for the job. An ephemeral runner removes the files and the processes that a job leaves on the machine of the runner before the next job, and the code of a pull request still reaches the network of the runner while the job runs.

forking takes read access, generally: the collaborators of the repository, and for an internal one every member of the enterprise reads it
the pull request runs with nobody doing anything

undetected_forms.text: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/<file>@<ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form

examples.name: remote-callee.yml
examples.text:
# situation: a job calls the reusable workflow .github/workflows/w.yml of
#   the repository example-org/self-hosted-runner-unanswered, whose content

#   with on: workflow_call in place of the on of private.yml. The linter has
#   no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
# reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event
#   that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read
#   the reusable workflow.
# cause: the rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from
#   the answer of workflow.definition.

#   whose copy of this workflow runs a step of their own in place of make.
# attack-run-behavior: the setting Run workflows from fork pull requests is
#   on, so the pull request's run starts; the job a runs the attacker's step
#   on a runner of the repository with both labels, where what it leaves

on: pull_request
permissions: {}
jobs:

inconclusive_kinds.text: a label of runs-on with a ${{ }} that refers to an input of workflow_dispatch (inputs, github.event.inputs), alone or in a string with other text: whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the value of the input. The rule reports the value in a job with an environment that has required reviewers too, where a required reviewer of the environment can stop the run

examples.name: input-dispatch.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on workflow_dispatch, runs-on is ${{ inputs.runner }}.
# reason: the one who dispatches the workflow chooses the value of the input
#   runner, and the workflow does not tell who dispatches, so whether an
#   attacker chooses the label is not known; nothing that the rule could
#   read is expected to tell who dispatches.
# attack: the attacker of this attack is the author of a pull request from a
#   fork, not the one who dispatches the workflow. When a dispatch gives the
#   input runner the label of a self-hosted runner of the repository, such
#   as self-hosted, the attacker opens a pull request from a fork whose
#   workflow runs a step of their own on runs-on: self-hosted.
# attack-run-behavior: a dispatch with runner set to self-hosted runs the
#   job a on that runner; the attacker's pull_request run, from the workflow
#   their pull request writes, is picked up by a runner with that label too,
#   and their step runs on that machine, where what it leaves stays for the
#   jobs after it, such as this one when dispatched again. With a label of a
#   runner GitHub hosts, such as ubuntu-latest, the job runs on a machine
#   discarded after it.
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      runner: {type: string}
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ${{ inputs.runner }}
    steps:
      - run: echo

#   attacker writes the name or the email of the pusher.
# attack: the author of a pull request writes x ##[set-output
#   name=tag;]$(id) in the name or the email of the account of the author, and
#   an account that can merge merges the pull request.
# attack-run-behavior: for a merge commit and for a squash, the pusher of
#   the push that the merge makes is the account that merged the pull request,
#   so the step prints the name and the email of the account that merged the
#   pull request, and the runner sets no output from the account of the
#   author.
on: push
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "pushed by ${{ github.event.pusher.name }} <${{ github.event.pusher.email }}>"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on push, the step p prints the name and the email of the pusher, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
notes.reason: the pusher is the account that pushed, or, for a push that the merge of a pull request makes, the account that merged the pull request. A push and a merge need a credential that can push or merge, such as an account with the role write or above, and the credential premise assumes that no attacker holds such a credential when the attack starts, so no attacker writes the name or the email of the pusher.
notes.attack: the author of a pull request writes x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id) in the name or the email of the account of the author, and an account that can merge merges the pull request.
notes.attack_run_behavior: for a merge commit and for a squash, the pusher of the push that the merge makes is the account that merged the pull request, so the step prints the name and the email of the account that merged the pull request, and the runner sets no output from the account of the author.

true_negatives.name: controlled.yml
true_negatives.text:
# situation: on issues, a step with no id prints the title of the issue.
# reason: the runner keeps the outputs of a step only when the step has
#   an id, so a set-output command in the title sets nothing that a
#   later step reads.
# attack: the attacker opens an issue titled x ##[set-output
#   name=tag;]$(id).
# attack-run-behavior: the runner warns that set-output is deprecated,
#   and no step reads an output of the step.
on: issues
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: |
          echo "issue: $TITLE"
      - run: echo next

notes.situation: on issues, a step with no id prints the title of the issue.
notes.reason: the runner keeps the outputs of a step only when the step has an id, so a set-output command in the title sets nothing that a later step reads.
notes.attack: the attacker opens an issue titled x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id).
notes.attack_run_behavior: the runner warns that set-output is deprecated, and no step reads an output of the step.

undetected_forms.text: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment that runs only for a pull request from a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository: the run of a review that the attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (repo.fork-pr-secrets, repo.fork-pr-write-tokens). The rule does not read the facts repo.fork-pr-secrets and repo.fork-pr-write-tokens for the runs of a review, and does not count the run of a review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker. When the attacker opened the pull request from a fork, a review of that pull request gives the attacker nothing more than the pull request itself gives: the run takes the workflow of the merge commit of the pull request (GitHub's documentation gives refs/pull/<n>/merge as the ref of the run of a review), and the attacker can change that workflow in the pull request

examples.name: fork-review.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on comments on the diff, the step p prints the comment's body
#   and a later step passes the output tag of the step p to ./release.sh,
#   in a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork.
# reason: a todo (a fact): the job runs only for a pull request from a
#   fork. Where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes
#   to the runs of pull requests from forks, the run of a review that the
#   attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has
#   those secrets or that token, and the job runs for the attacker.
# cause: the rule does not read the settings of a private repository for
#   the runs of pull requests from forks, and does not count the run of a
#   review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "::set-output name=tag::v9.9.9-PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: the comment of the attacker on the diff of the pull
#   request of another person from a fork starts the job a; the runner
#   reads the printed line as the command set-output, and ./release.sh
#   gets v9.9.9-PWNED as the tag.
on: pull_request_review_comment
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name != github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          B: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "c=$B"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on comments on the diff, the step p prints the comment's body and a later step passes the output tag of the step p to ./release.sh, in a job that runs only for a pull request from a fork.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): the job runs only for a pull request from a fork. Where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks, the run of a review that the attacker writes on the pull request of another person from a fork has those secrets or that token, and the job runs for the attacker.
notes.cause: the rule does not read the settings of a private repository for the runs of pull requests from forks, and does not count the run of a review of a pull request from a fork as a run of the attacker.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the comment of the attacker on the diff of the pull request of another person from a fork starts the job a; the runner reads the printed line as the command set-output, and ./release.sh gets v9.9.9-PWNED as the tag.

undetected_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space. The if of the job limits the value in every step of the job, and the if of a step with a run: script limits the value in that step only. In those steps the value equals one of the strings when the case of the letters is ignored, so the rule does not report the value. The attacker still chooses the case of each letter of the value. GitHub's server, which evaluates the if of a job, also takes the Kelvin sign as equal to the letter k and the long s as equal to the letter s; the runner, which evaluates the if of a step, takes the Kelvin sign as equal to the letter k. Where the case of a letter changes what the value names, such as a command, a variable, a file on a file system that tells names apart by their case (the default file system of a Linux runner), a host or a tool, the choice of the case can cause harm

examples.name: if-compared.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment, a job runs only when the comment's body is
#   tag, and a step that has an id prints a set-output command whose name
#   is ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the step has an id, so the runner
#   sets the outputs of the step from the workflow commands that the step
#   prints.
# reason: the job's if lets the body be only the string tag, ignoring the
#   case of its letters, so the body is no workflow command; the attacker
#   still chooses the case of the name of the output, and the author of
#   this example has not checked whether the case of the name of an output
#   changes which output a later step reads.
# cause: the rule does not treat a value that the if of the job compares
#   with such a string as written by the attacker.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "TAG"
# attack-run-behavior: the if passes, and the step prints
#   ::set-output name=TAG::v1.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    if: github.event.comment.body == 'tag'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "::set-output name=${{ github.event.comment.body }}::v1"

notes.situation: on issue_comment, a job runs only when the comment's body is tag, and a step that has an id prints a set-output command whose name is ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the step has an id, so the runner sets the outputs of the step from the workflow commands that the step prints.
notes.reason: the job's if lets the body be only the string tag, ignoring the case of its letters, so the body is no workflow command; the attacker still chooses the case of the name of the output, and the author of this example has not checked whether the case of the name of an output changes which output a later step reads.
notes.cause: the rule does not treat a value that the if of the job compares with such a string as written by the attacker.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the if passes, and the step prints ::set-output name=TAG::v1.

undetected_forms.text: a job that runs only on pull_request, in one of two cases. In the first case, only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow: the author of a pull request can change the workflow itself, so the run of the job gives the author what the run has (read-only from a fork, or what a private repository sends to the runs of pull requests from forks: secrets, a token that writes) without the flaw of the rule, and the flaw of the rule adds nothing to what the author gets. In the second case, a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on the pull requests of its other repositories (Require workflows to pass before merging, of GitHub Enterprise): the author of such a pull request cannot change the workflow, and whether the run has more than the pull_request workflow of the author would get (the token, secrets) is known from GitHub's documentation only, as no such run was observed; making a required check pass is outside the threat model of the rule. The workflow does not say which case holds, and the rule does not read which case holds

examples.name: pull-request.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on pull_request, the step p prints the title of the pull
#   request, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p
#   into its script.
# reason: when only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow, the
#   author of the pull request can change the workflow itself and gets what the
#   run has without the flaw, so the flaw adds nothing to what the author gets;
#   when a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on
#   the pull requests of its other repositories, the author cannot change the
#   workflow, and what the run of the ruleset has beyond the author's own
#   pull_request workflow is not known. The workflow does not say which case
#   holds.
# cause: the rule does not count pull_request as an event of an attacker. The
#   rule does not read whether a ruleset runs the workflow.
# attack: the author of a pull request from a fork titles the pull
#   request x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id).
# attack-run-behavior: the runner sets the output tag, and the release step
#   runs id with what the run of the pull request has. When a ruleset of the
#   organization runs the workflow on a pull request of another repository, the
#   same steps run in the run of the ruleset; what the run of the ruleset has
#   was not observed, so whether the steps do harm in the run of the ruleset is
#   not known.
on: pull_request
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on pull_request, the step p prints the title of the pull request, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
notes.reason: when only the pull requests of the repository run the workflow, the author of the pull request can change the workflow itself and gets what the run has without the flaw, so the flaw adds nothing to what the author gets; when a ruleset of the organization or the enterprise runs the workflow on the pull requests of its other repositories, the author cannot change the workflow, and what the run of the ruleset has beyond the author's own pull_request workflow is not known. The workflow does not say which case holds.
notes.cause: the rule does not count pull_request as an event of an attacker. The rule does not read whether a ruleset runs the workflow.
notes.attack: the author of a pull request from a fork titles the pull request x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id).
notes.attack_run_behavior: the runner sets the output tag, and the release step runs id with what the run of the pull request has. When a ruleset of the organization runs the workflow on a pull request of another repository, the same steps run in the run of the ruleset; what the run of the ruleset has was not observed, so whether the steps do harm in the run of the ruleset is not known.

undetected_forms.text: a value of the event of workflow_dispatch other than its inputs, in a job that runs only on workflow_dispatch: the event has the ref, which is a branch or a tag that the repository already has, and values that GitHub fills, such as the login of the account that dispatches the workflow; the event has no text of an issue, a comment or a pull request. Whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and nothing else of the event. A token that cannot change the files of the repository can dispatch the workflow, such as a fine-grained token that has the permission Actions with write access and no permission Contents. The rule reports an input of the dispatch with the inconclusive kind input-dispatch

examples.name: dispatch.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on workflow_dispatch, the step p prints the title of the issue,
#   and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its
#   script. If the workflow also ran on issues, the rule would report the
#   same steps.
# reason: no added gain: on workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object,
#   so the expression of the title gives an empty string; whoever dispatches
#   the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and the steps
#   read no input.
# cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads does not
#   have workflow_dispatch; the rule reports an input of a dispatch with the
#   inconclusive kind input-dispatch.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id)"
# attack-run-behavior: with the value put in, the step prints the value, the
#   runner sets the output tag of the step to $(id), and the release step
#   writes the output into its script and runs id. On workflow_dispatch the
#   event has no issue object, though: the expression gives an empty string,
#   and the step prints an empty line.
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ github.event.issue.title }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on workflow_dispatch, the step p prints the title of the issue, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script. If the workflow also ran on issues, the rule would report the same steps.
notes.reason: no added gain: on workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object, so the expression of the title gives an empty string; whoever dispatches the workflow chooses the ref and the inputs of the dispatch, and the steps read no input.
notes.cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads does not have workflow_dispatch; the rule reports an input of a dispatch with the inconclusive kind input-dispatch.
notes.attack_run_behavior: with the value put in, the step prints the value, the runner sets the output tag of the step to $(id), and the release step writes the output into its script and runs id. On workflow_dispatch the event has no issue object, though: the expression gives an empty string, and the step prints an empty line.

undetected_forms.text: a value of the client_payload of repository_dispatch (github.event.client_payload): only a credential with write access to the permission Contents of the repository can send repository_dispatch, and the credential premise assumes that no attacker holds such a credential; the sender chooses the whole client_payload

examples.name: repository-dispatch.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on repository_dispatch, the step p prints the value title of
#   the client_payload, and the release step writes the output tag of the step
#   p into its script.
# reason: the form adds nothing to what the attacker gets (the disposition
#   no-added-gain): only a credential with write access to the permission
#   Contents of the repository can send repository_dispatch, and the
#   credential premise assumes that no attacker holds such a credential; the
#   sender chooses the whole client_payload.
# cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads leaves out
#   repository_dispatch on purpose: the credential premise leaves the sender
#   of repository_dispatch out of the threat model.
# attack-value: github.event.client_payload.title = "x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id)"
# attack-run-behavior: when a repository_dispatch with the value in its
#   client_payload runs the workflow, the step p prints the value, the runner
#   sets the output tag of the step p to $(id), and the release step writes
#   the output into its script and runs id.
on: repository_dispatch
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ github.event.client_payload.title }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on repository_dispatch, the step p prints the value title of the client_payload, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
notes.reason: the form adds nothing to what the attacker gets (the disposition no-added-gain): only a credential with write access to the permission Contents of the repository can send repository_dispatch, and the credential premise assumes that no attacker holds such a credential; the sender chooses the whole client_payload.
notes.cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads leaves out repository_dispatch on purpose: the credential premise leaves the sender of repository_dispatch out of the threat model.
notes.attack_run_behavior: when a repository_dispatch with the value in its client_payload runs the workflow, the step p prints the value, the runner sets the output tag of the step p to $(id), and the release step writes the output into its script and runs id.

undetected_forms.text: a value that an app outside GitHub Actions writes into a field of a commit status or a check run (the fields context, description and target_url of status; the fields name, output, details_url and external_id of check_run): the app may copy a value of a pull request from a fork into the field, such as the name of a job that a configuration file of the pull request gives to an outside CI; the rule reads the field as a field whose value the app chooses

examples.name: app-written.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on check_run, which an app outside GitHub Actions starts when
#   the app makes a check run for a commit, the job writes the name of the
#   check run (github.event.check_run.name) where the rule reads it.
# reason: a todo (a fact): the app writes the name of the check run, and an
#   app may copy a value of a pull request from a fork into the name, such
#   as the name of a job that a configuration file of the pull request gives
#   to an outside CI.
# cause: the table of what an attacker controls reads the values that the
#   app writes into a commit status or a check run as the values that the
#   app chooses.
# attack-value: github.event.check_run.name = "::set-output name=tag::v9"
# attack-run-behavior: an outside CI copies the name of a job from the
#   configuration file of the pull request from a fork into the name of the
#   check run; the run of check_run starts on the default branch, and the
#   value does there what the attack value of the message of the commit does
#   on status.
on: check_run
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ github.event.check_run.name }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on check_run, which an app outside GitHub Actions starts when the app makes a check run for a commit, the job writes the name of the check run (github.event.check_run.name) where the rule reads it.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): the app writes the name of the check run, and an app may copy a value of a pull request from a fork into the name, such as the name of a job that a configuration file of the pull request gives to an outside CI.
notes.cause: the table of what an attacker controls reads the values that the app writes into a commit status or a check run as the values that the app chooses.
notes.attack_run_behavior: an outside CI copies the name of a job from the configuration file of the pull request from a fork into the name of the check run; the run of check_run starts on the default branch, and the value does there what the attack value of the message of the commit does on status.

undetected_forms.text: a value of the payload of deployment_status, such as the SHA of the deployment (deployment.sha), when an app outside GitHub Actions makes a deployment and a status of the deployment for a commit of a pull request from a fork: no run of deployment_status started when the authors of the linter tried this, and why the run did not start was not found; the rule does not read deployment_status as an event that an attacker starts

examples.name: deployment-status.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on deployment_status, which an app outside GitHub Actions
#   starts when the app makes a status of a deployment, the job writes the
#   description of the deployment (github.event.deployment.description)
#   where the rule reads it.
# reason: a todo (a fact): no run of deployment_status started when a GitHub
#   App made a deployment and a status of the deployment for a commit of a
#   pull request from a fork (seen on GitHub), and why the run did not start
#   was not found.
# cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads does not
#   have deployment_status.
# attack-value: github.event.deployment.description = "::set-output name=tag::v9"
# attack-run-behavior: an outside app makes a deployment for the commit of
#   the pull request from a fork with a description that the pull request
#   gives, and a status of the deployment; if a run of deployment_status

on: deployment_status
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ github.event.deployment.description }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on deployment_status, which an app outside GitHub Actions starts when the app makes a status of a deployment, the job writes the description of the deployment (github.event.deployment.description) where the rule reads it.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): no run of deployment_status started when a GitHub App made a deployment and a status of the deployment for a commit of a pull request from a fork (seen on GitHub), and why the run did not start was not found.
notes.cause: the table of the attacker's events that the rule reads does not have deployment_status.
notes.attack_run_behavior: an outside app makes a deployment for the commit of the pull request from a fork with a description that the pull request gives, and a status of the deployment; if a run of deployment_status starts on the default branch, the value does there what the attack value of the message of the commit does on status.

undetected_forms.text: a workflow on an event of an attacker that puts a value the attacker writes into the client_payload of a repository_dispatch that the workflow sends (gh api with client_payload to the endpoint dispatches, peter-evans/repository-dispatch), and a workflow on repository_dispatch that uses the value: the flaw is in the workflow that sends the repository_dispatch, and the rule does not read what a workflow sends to another workflow

examples.name: .github/workflows/receiver.yml
examples.text:
# situation: sender.yml runs on issues opened, and with the GITHUB_TOKEN
#   sends a repository_dispatch of the type relay whose client_payload has the
#   title of the issue as the value title; receiver.yml runs on that
#   repository_dispatch, and the step p prints the value title of the
#   client_payload, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p
#   into its script.
# reason: the author of the issue writes the value, and sender.yml relays
#   the value to receiver.yml in a repository_dispatch that a run of the
#   repository sends with a token of the repository; GitHub creates a workflow
#   run for a repository_dispatch sent with the GITHUB_TOKEN, as an exception
#   to the rule that an event that the GITHUB_TOKEN triggers creates no
#   workflow run.
# cause: the rule reads the events of each workflow alone, and does not read
#   what a workflow sends to another workflow as the client_payload of a
#   repository_dispatch.
# attack-value: github.event.issue.title = "x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id)"
# attack-run-behavior: the attacker opens an issue whose title is the value;
#   sender.yml sends the value, and in the run of receiver.yml the step p
#   prints the value, the runner sets the output tag of the step p to $(id),
#   and the release step writes the output into its script and runs id.
on:
  repository_dispatch:
    types: [relay]
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ github.event.client_payload.title }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

others.name: .github/workflows/sender.yml
others.text:
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  relay:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          VALUE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: gh api "repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/dispatches" -f event_type=relay -f "client_payload[title]=$VALUE"

notes.situation: sender.yml runs on issues opened, and with the GITHUB_TOKEN sends a repository_dispatch of the type relay whose client_payload has the title of the issue as the value title; receiver.yml runs on that repository_dispatch, and the step p prints the value title of the client_payload, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
notes.reason: the author of the issue writes the value, and sender.yml relays the value to receiver.yml in a repository_dispatch that a run of the repository sends with a token of the repository; GitHub creates a workflow run for a repository_dispatch sent with the GITHUB_TOKEN, as an exception to the rule that an event that the GITHUB_TOKEN triggers creates no workflow run.
notes.cause: the rule reads the events of each workflow alone, and does not read what a workflow sends to another workflow as the client_payload of a repository_dispatch.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the attacker opens an issue whose title is the value; sender.yml sends the value, and in the run of receiver.yml the step p prints the value, the runner sets the output tag of the step p to $(id), and the release step writes the output into its script and runs id.

undetected_forms.text: an input of workflow_dispatch that a caller of the same repository passes, as an input of the call (under the key with: of the calling job or step), to a reusable workflow or a composite action, which uses the input as a value: the one who dispatches the caller chooses the value, and the rule reads the events of a called workflow or action from the table of the callers, and does not follow the value of an input of workflow_dispatch that the caller gives

examples.name: .github/workflows/called.yml
examples.text:
# situation: caller.yml runs on workflow_dispatch with the input x, and
#   calls called.yml with the input x of the dispatch as the input x of
#   called.yml; called.yml prints the input x in the step p, and the release
#   step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
# reason: the one who dispatches caller.yml chooses the value:
#   input-dispatch reports such a value where a workflow on workflow_dispatch
#   refers to its input directly, but through the call the value is the input
#   x of called.yml.
# cause: the rule reads the events of a called workflow from the table of
#   the callers, and does not follow the value of an input of
#   workflow_dispatch that a caller gives in with.
# attack-value: inputs.x = "x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id)"
# attack-run-behavior: when the one who dispatches caller.yml gives the
#   value as x, the step p prints the value, the runner sets the output tag of
#   the step p to $(id), and the release step writes the output into its
#   script and runs id.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      x: {type: string}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        run: echo "${{ inputs.x }}"

examples.name: not-attacker.yml

# situation: on issues, the step p prints the variable RELEASE_TAG and the
#   secret RELEASE_NOTE, which reach the step through env. The step p also
#   prints runner.os. The release step writes the output tag of the step p
#   into its script.

#   vars, secrets or runner.os, and one who may change the repository's
#   settings sets the variable and the secret. A run of the linter that adds
#   variables-writer (--add-attacker) reports the variable, a run that adds
#   secrets-writer reports the secret, and no run reports runner.os.
# cause: the rule does not count vars, secrets and runner as values of an
#   attacker.
# attack: one who may change the repository's settings sets RELEASE_TAG to
#   x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id); in a run that adds no attacker, no
#   attacker can set the variable.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints the values; no attacker sets the
#   output tag.
on: issues
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          TAG: ${{ vars.RELEASE_TAG }}
          NOTE: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_NOTE }}
        run: |
          echo "tag: $TAG"
          echo "note: $NOTE"
          echo "${{ runner.os }}"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

A run of the linter that adds variables-writer (--add-attacker) reports the variable, a run that adds secrets-writer reports the secret, and no run reports runner.os.

notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints the values; no attacker sets the output tag.

examples.name: .github/workflows/called.yml

# situation: the workflow is called; the step p prints

on:

permissions: {}

undetected_forms.text: an if that lets in MEMBER or COLLABORATOR by the author_association of the issue, the pull request or the discussion the run is of, which the following pass: a member or a collaborator whose repository role is Read only, who gets, in the run, a token that writes and the secrets, more than what the Read role gives; the account of such a member or collaborator, taken over; and an outsider who becomes a MEMBER with the Read role, in an organization that lets anyone become a member (a bot that invites whoever asks). A member or a collaborator whose role is Triage or above holds a credential that can add a label or write to the repository, which the credential premise assumes no attacker holds. Who is a member, and with what role, is not in the workflow

examples.name: insider-association.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues opened, a job whose if lets in an issue whose
#   author_association is MEMBER prints the body of the issue in the
#   step p, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p
#   into its script.
# reason: a todo (a fact): a member of the organization, who may have read
#   access only, passes this if (in an organization that lets anyone become a
#   member, such as by a bot that invites whoever asks, an outsider becomes such
#   a member), and gets the token and the secrets of the job past what the Read
#   role gives; who is a member, and with what role, is not in the workflow.
# cause: the rule evaluates the if with the attacker's
#   author_association (NONE, FIRST_TIMER, FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR or
#   CONTRIBUTOR), for which the if is false, so no attacker's event runs
#   the job.
# attack: a member whose role is read opens an issue whose body is x
#   ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id).

#   runner sets the output tag, and the release step runs id. On an
#   issue whose author_association is NONE, FIRST_TIMER,
#   FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR or CONTRIBUTOR, the if skips the job.

  issues:
    types: [opened]
permissions: {}
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.issue.author_association == 'MEMBER'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: echo "$BODY"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on issues opened, a job whose if lets in an issue whose author_association is MEMBER prints the body of the issue in the step p, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): a member of the organization, who may have read access only, passes this if (in an organization that lets anyone become a member, such as by a bot that invites whoever asks, an outsider becomes such a member), and gets the token and the secrets of the job past what the Read role gives; who is a member, and with what role, is not in the workflow.
notes.cause: the rule evaluates the if with the attacker's author_association (NONE, FIRST_TIMER, FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR or CONTRIBUTOR), for which the if is false, so no attacker's event runs the job.
notes.attack: a member whose role is read opens an issue whose body is x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id).
notes.attack_run_behavior: on an issue a member opens, the job runs, the runner sets the output tag, and the release step runs id. On an issue whose author_association is NONE, FIRST_TIMER, FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR or CONTRIBUTOR, the if skips the job.

undetected_forms.text: a job or a step inside a reusable workflow of another repository (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/<file>@<ref>) whose content the fact workflow.definition does not give. For every rule: a run that does not ask the fact (a run without --online and without the answer in --facts). For a quality rule, also: a run where the linter asked the fact and got no answer (an answer of unknown: the GitHub API did not give the file), and a call deeper than the 3 levels of reusable workflows that the linter reads, for which the linter does not ask the fact. The rule reads a reusable workflow of another repository only from the answer of workflow.definition. For a rule that is not a quality rule (a rule with a threat), the last two forms are the inconclusive kind remote-callee-unknown, not this form

on: issues
permissions: {}
jobs:
  c:

The linter has no answer of the fact workflow.definition for the reusable workflow.
notes.reason: a todo (a fact): the jobs of a reusable workflow run on the event that started the run of the calling job, and the linter does not read the reusable workflow.

inconclusive_kinds.text: a value where whether an attacker can write ##[ and ] in the value was not checked, such as a structured value (a URL, or github.event.forkee.description, which is the description of a fork; the account that makes the fork writes the description, and the description holds no line break). Two kinds of structured value are not of this kind: the email of a git commit, which was checked to hold ##[ and ] and is reported, and the names of refs and repositories, which hold no [ and are not reported. The name of a wiki page (page_name) is of this kind. For a page made on the web interface of GitHub, the page name holds no blank, because GitHub turns each blank of the title into a - after trimming the blanks at the head and the end of the title; a set-output command needs a blank between the word set-output and the property name=, so the page name holds no set-output command. For a page pushed by git, the page name keeps each blank and - of the file name of the page and can hold a set-output command, and a push by git from an account with the role read or triage was not tried (GitHub refused a push by git from an account with no role in the repository). The rule cannot tell from the value which way the page was made. Any other value that an attacker controls on gollum alone is of this kind too, such as github.event.pages[0][x] where x is an expression, or toJSON(github.event). The title of a wiki page is not of this kind: the title holds no -, so the title as written holds no command whose name has a -, and the rule reports nothing on the title (a command that decodes escapes can make a - of the title: decoded-escape)

examples.name: structured-value.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on fork, the step p prints the description of the fork that
#   the fork event is about, and the release step writes the output tag of
#   the step p into its script.
# reason: the account that makes the fork writes the description of the
#   fork, and whether GitHub takes ##[ and ] in the description of a fork
#   was not checked; GitHub refused a line break in the description of a
#   fork.
# cause: the table of what an attacker controls reads the description of
#   a fork as structured, and the characters that GitHub takes in the
#   description of a fork were not checked on GitHub.
# attack: an attacker forks the repository and writes x ##[set-output
#   name=tag;]$(id) as the description of the fork.
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints the description of the fork; were
#   the description the attacker's x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id), the
#   runner would set the output tag of the step p, and the release step
#   would run id.
on: fork
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          DESCRIPTION: ${{ github.event.forkee.description }}
        run: echo "forked as $DESCRIPTION"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.cause: the table of what an attacker controls reads the description of a fork as structured, and the characters that GitHub takes in the description of a fork were not checked on GitHub.
notes.attack: an attacker forks the repository and writes x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id) as the description of the fork.
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints the description of the fork; were the description the attacker's x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id), the runner would set the output tag of the step p, and the release step would run id.

false_positive_forms.text: a variable of the env of the step that the script sets again in the last command of a pipeline after a shopt -s lastpipe whose option name the script does not write as a literal word (shopt -s "$o"): bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the shell that runs the pipeline, so after the pipeline the variable holds the value that the script sets, and the rule reads the variable as holding the value of the env

examples.name: lastpipe-not-literal.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issues, the step p passes the title of the issue in the
#   environment variable TITLE, turns lastpipe on with shopt -s and the
#   option name in a variable, sets TITLE to a fixed word with read in the

#   the output tag of the step p into its script.
# reason: with lastpipe, bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the
#   shell that runs the pipeline, so TITLE holds the fixed word when echo
#   runs, and the step does not print the title.
# cause: the rule follows lastpipe only after shopt -s lastpipe written as
#   literal words, so the rule reads TITLE as holding the value of the env.
# attack: the attacker opens an issue titled x ##[set-output
#   name=tag;]$(id).
# attack-run-behavior: the step prints "issue: safe", the output tag stays
#   empty, and the release step runs with an empty tag.
on: issues
permissions: {}
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: |
          o=lastpipe
          shopt -s "$o"
          echo safe | read -r TITLE
          echo "issue: $TITLE"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on issues, the step p passes the title of the issue in the environment variable TITLE, turns lastpipe on with shopt -s and the option name in a variable, sets TITLE to a fixed word with read in the last command of a pipeline, and prints TITLE; the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.
notes.reason: with lastpipe, bash runs the last command of the pipeline in the shell that runs the pipeline, so TITLE holds the fixed word when echo runs, and the step does not print the title.

notes.attack: the attacker opens an issue titled x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id).
notes.attack_run_behavior: the step prints "issue: safe", the output tag stays empty, and the release step runs with an empty tag.

false_positive_forms.text: a job on pull_request_review or pull_request_review_comment whose if: condition lets the job run only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork, such as a job whose if: condition is github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork: on a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. The run of a review of a pull request from a fork has the secrets of the repository or a token that writes only where a private repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review). The rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reports the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository

examples.name: fork-flag-review.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on comments on the diff, the step p prints the comment's body
#   and a later step passes the output tag of the step p to ./release.sh,
#   in a job that runs only when the head repository of the pull request
#   is a fork.
# reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request
#   is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head
#   repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a
#   fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In
#   a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a
#   token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither
#   secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or
#   a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the
#   undetected form fork-review).
# cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the
#   workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and
#   reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a
#   branch of the repository.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "::set-output name=tag::v9.9.9-PWNED"
# attack-run-behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review
#   of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the
#   job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository
#   itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no
#   secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret
#   and no token that writes.
on: pull_request_review_comment
jobs:
  a:
    if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          B: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "c=$B"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: on comments on the diff, the step p prints the comment's body and a later step passes the output tag of the step p to ./release.sh, in a job that runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork.
notes.reason: the job runs only when the head repository of the pull request is a fork. On a pull request from a branch of the repository, the head repository is the repository itself, so in a repository that is not a fork the job runs only for a review of a pull request from a fork. In a public repository, the run of such a review has no secrets and a token that only reads; in a private repository, the run has neither secrets nor a token that writes unless the repository gives secrets or a token that writes to the runs of pull requests from forks (the undetected form fork-review).
notes.cause: the rule does not read whether the repository that runs the workflow (not the head repository of the pull request) is a fork, and reads the job as if the job ran for a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository.
notes.attack_run_behavior: in a public repository that is not a fork, a review of a pull request from a branch of the repository does not start the job, as the head repository of such a pull request is the repository itself; a review of a pull request from a fork starts the job with no secrets and a token that only reads, so the value reaches no secret and no token that writes.

false_positive_forms.text: a string only those who can write to the repository, or moderate or administer its organization, set, which the webhook schema leaves free and the table reads as arbitrary, such as the name of a label (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/using-labels-and-milestones-to-track-work/managing-labels), the reason a comment is hidden (https://docs.github.com/en/communities/moderating-comments-and-conversations/managing-disruptive-comments), the name of an issue field or of its option (https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/using-issues/managing-issue-fields-in-your-organization)

notes.situation: on issues, the step p prints the name of the label of the event, and the release step writes the output tag of the step p into its script.

false_positive_forms.text: a value that an if compares with strings that the workflow writes in the if (strings compared by == with the value and joined by ||, or the strings of contains(fromJSON('[...]'), value)), where each string has only ASCII letters, digits, spaces, -, _, . and /, does not start with -, and has no - right after a space, where the rule reports the value although the if limits the value to those strings, because the rule does not read the if in one of three forms. (1) A reusable workflow or a composite action gets the value through an input, and the if of the calling job or the calling step compares the value. The rule reports the value in the file of the reusable workflow or the composite action. The value is harmless when the if of every caller of that file, inside and outside the repository, compares the value. (2) The if compares the value under one name, and the script writes the value under another name: for example, the if compares env.BODY, which the env of the step sets to ${{ github.event.comment.body }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; or the if compares ${{ github.head_ref }}, and the script writes ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.ref }}. The value is harmless when the two names hold the same value in the step; the rule does not check that the two names hold the same value. (3) The if of a step that uses an action compares a value that the with or the env of the same step holds. At the start of the job, the runner runs the pre step of each action from another repository whose action.yml has runs.pre, under the condition runs.pre-if of that action.yml and not under the if of the step. For the pre step, the runner evaluates the with and the env of the step, and the code of the pre step may read the inputs. The runner runs no pre step of a local action (./). The value is harmless when the action has no pre step, or when the code of the pre step does not read the value. In each form, the value is harmless only where the case of the letters does not change what the value names (the undetected form if-compared)

examples.name: if-unnarrowed.yml
examples.text:
# situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in
#   env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step prints
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the step has an id, so the runner
#   sets the outputs of the step from the workflow commands that the step
#   prints.
# reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body,
#   with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its
#   letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no
#   line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
# cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if
#   compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes
#   ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY
#   holds the comment's body.
# attack-value: github.event.comment.body = "x ##[set-output name=tag;]$(id)"
# attack-run-behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body,
#   and the runner skips the step.
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  j:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        if: env.BODY == 'deploy'
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}
        run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}"

notes.situation: on issue_comment created, a step that has the comment's body in env.BODY runs only when env.BODY is deploy, and the step prints ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the step has an id, so the runner sets the outputs of the step from the workflow commands that the step prints.
notes.reason: the step's if compares env.BODY, which holds the comment's body, with deploy, so in the step the body is deploy, ignoring the case of its letters: the body has no character that the shell reads as code, no line break, no word that starts with - and no workflow command.
notes.cause: the rule limits a value by an if only under the name that the if compares: the if compares env.BODY, and the script writes ${{ github.event.comment.body }}; the rule does not check that env.BODY holds the comment's body.
notes.attack_run_behavior: on GitHub, the step's if is false for such a body, and the runner skips the step.

false_positive_forms.text: a step that is not a background step, and whose run script also writes name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT for each output name that is read later, by the steps after the step, by the outputs of the job or by the outputs of the action. The run script writes each such name outside every if, case and ||, so that the write runs on every path of the script. The runner reads $GITHUB_OUTPUT when the step is done, and the value in $GITHUB_OUTPUT replaces the value from the log. A reference that does not name an output (toJSON(steps.<id>.outputs), toJSON(steps), steps[...]) reads every output name, the names that the attacker chooses among them, so a step whose outputs are read through such a reference is not of this form

permissions: {}

notes.reason: the runner sets the outputs of $GITHUB_OUTPUT after the step, over the outputs of the log, so the release step gets the tag of the file.
notes.cause: the rule does not read which output names the steps after the step read, nor what the step writes to $GITHUB_OUTPUT.

false_positive_forms.text: a reusable workflow or a composite action when all of the following are true: the rule does not know all of the callers of the reusable workflow or the composite action; every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action (directly, or through another reusable workflow or composite action) is a workflow in the same repository; and the rule would report no finding of the finding kind if the rule read the reusable workflow or the composite action only on the events on which the workflows in the same repository run the reusable workflow or the composite action (for example, every workflow that runs the reusable workflow or the composite action runs only on push). When the rule does not know all of the callers, the rule can read the reusable workflow or the composite action on every event (the worst case). For example, the rule does not know all of the callers when no caller is among the inputs; when the inputs are not the whole repository; for a composite action, when an input is excluded or cannot be read; when a caller names the reusable workflow or the composite action by a name of the form owner/repo/path@ref instead of by a ./ path, in which owner/repo is the repository that the --repo flag names, or is any repository when no --repo flag is given; when a step names the composite action by a ./ path, and either no checkout step runs before that step or the last checkout step before that step is not a plain checkout step (a plain checkout step has no ref input, no repository input and no path input); when a step inside a composite action names another composite action by a ./ path; or when the rule does not know all of the callers of a caller

examples.name: callee.yml
examples.text:
# situation: a reusable workflow prints the title of an issue in the step p,
#   whose output tag the release step writes into its script, and only the
#   repository's own workflows call the reusable workflow, all of them on
#   push.
# reason: the issue the workflow reads is never an outsider's.
# cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
# attack: an outsider cannot start a caller on issues.
# attack-run-behavior: called on push, the event has no issue, so the step
#   prints an empty line and sets no output.
on: workflow_call
permissions: {}
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          V: ${{ github.event.issue.title }}
        run: echo "$V"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

notes.situation: a reusable workflow prints the title of an issue in the step p, whose output tag the release step writes into its script, and only the repository's own workflows call the reusable workflow, all of them on push.
notes.reason: the issue the workflow reads is never an outsider's.
notes.cause: a callee is read in the worst case, as if a caller ran on issues.
notes.attack: an outsider cannot start a caller on issues.
notes.attack_run_behavior: called on push, the event has no issue, so the step prints an empty line and sets no output.

examples.name: .github/workflows/called.yml
examples.text:
# situation: ci.yml of the repository o/r calls this reusable workflow on
#   push only, by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main, not by the
#   path ./.github/workflows/called.yml.
# reason: when the run of the linter names the repository (--repo o/r), the
#   call by the name is a call of this file, and the only caller runs on
#   push, which no attacker of the finding kind triggers. A run without
#   --repo reads the call by the name o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
#   as a call that may name a file of the repository, because the run does
#   not know which repository the inputs are; the rule does not resolve the
#   call to this file, so the rule reads this file on every event and reports
#   the same finding.
# cause: the rule does not resolve a call by the name of the repository to
#   the file, so the rule reads this workflow on every event.
# attack: the attacker opens an issue, a pull request or a comment with a
#   value that would reach this workflow on an event of the attacker.
# attack-run-behavior: only a push to the repository runs ci.yml, which
#   calls this workflow on push; the run of the push reads no value of the
#   attacker's issue, pull request or comment.
on:
  workflow_call:
permissions: {}
jobs:
  a:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - id: p
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.issue.body }}
        run: echo "$BODY"
      - run: ./release.sh "${{ steps.p.outputs.tag }}"

others.name: .github/workflows/ci.yml
others.text:
on: push
jobs:
  call:
    uses: o/r/.github/workflows/called.yml@main
    secrets: inherit

false_positive_forms.text: a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and no other event (no workflow_call event either), in a repository whose Actions policies block the runs of the workflow on pull_request_target (repo.pull-request-target-allowed false): an event policy that an administrator sets without pull_request_target among the allowed events, or the default policy that GitHub adds to a public repository without an applicable event policy, from the time when GitHub enforces the default policy on the repository. GitHub's documents say that GitHub evaluates the policies before a run, and that a run that a policy does not allow fails with an error. The documents do not say whether a job of such a run starts before the run fails; the rule assumes that no job of such a run starts

false_positive_forms.text: a run that the Actions policies of the repository block, in four cases where the rule does not take the policies into account. First, an event policy that blocks an event of the attackers other than pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) in a workflow whose on has that event: the rules ask a fact only for pull_request_target. Second, an actor rule that does not allow the account of the attacker (for example, an actor rule that allows only the repository roles with write access): repo.pull-request-target-allowed is one value for all the runs of a workflow file on pull_request_target, and an actor rule blocks a run by the account that starts the run, so the fact cannot tell what an actor rule blocks. Third, a workflow whose on has pull_request_target and another event: the rule does not ask repo.pull-request-target-allowed for such a workflow, because a run on the other event can reach the job. When the if of the job is false on the other event, so that the job runs only on pull_request_target, and a policy blocks pull_request_target, the finding is a false positive. Fourth, a reusable workflow (on workflow_call) or an action that only workflows on pull_request_target call: the rule asks repo.pull-request-target-allowed only of a workflow whose on has pull_request_target, not of the reusable workflow or the action, so a finding in the reusable workflow or the action is still reported when the policies block the runs of every caller
